components.note: 忄 (heart) — dread and apprehension are feelings, fittingly written with the heart radical.
单 (dān) gives a sound close to 惮's reading dàn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他做事肆无忌惮。
example.pinyin: Tā zuòshì sìwú jìdàn.
example.english: He does things recklessly, without any restraint.
example.fact: 惮 rarely stands alone in modern Chinese — it survives mainly in the idiom 肆无忌惮 (sìwú jìdàn), 'reckless and unrestrained.'

components.note: 气 (gas/vapor) — 氖 names a gaseous element.
乃 (nǎi) gives the sound — an exact match with 氖's reading.

example.hanzi: 氖气发出的光是橙红色的。
example.pinyin: Nǎiqì fāchū de guāng shì chéng hóng sè de.
example.english: The light given off by neon gas is orange-red.
example.fact: Neon signs glow orange-red because that is the color neon gas emits naturally when electrified — other colors in so-called 'neon signs' actually come from different gases.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 捎 describes carrying or delivering something by hand.
肖 (xiào) is the traditional phonetic element, though its modern reading has drifted further from 捎's shāo than most phonetic pairs.

example.hanzi: 我出差的时候能帮你捎点东西回来。
example.pinyin: Wǒ chūchāi de shíhou néng bāng nǐ shāo diǎn dōngxi huílái.
example.english: When I go on a business trip I can bring some things back for you.
example.fact: 捎 often pairs with 带 in 捎带 (shāodài) — bringing something along as a small favor while already doing something else, a concept with no single English word.

components.note: 羊 (sheep) — 羔 specifically names a young sheep, a lamb.
灬 (a form of 火, fire) sits beneath the sheep; rather than giving a sound close to gāo, most accounts read the whole character as 'sheep over fire' — an old image tied to preparing lamb meat.

example.hanzi: 羔羊温顺地跟着母羊。
example.pinyin: Gāoyáng wēnshùn de gēnzhe mǔ yáng.
example.english: The lamb gently follows the ewe.
example.fact: In traditional Chinese sayings, a lamb kneeling to nurse from its mother — 羊有跪乳之恩 — is used as a classical symbol of filial gratitude.

etymologyHint: A person 亻 waiting for something to finish 矣; 矣 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (a person) — 俟 describes someone waiting.

矣 is a classical sentence-final particle marking completion; paired with 亻, the image is of a person standing by until something finishes — its own reading (yǐ) isn't close to 俟's, so the pairing works through meaning rather than sound.

example.hanzi: 万俟是中国古代的一个复姓。
example.pinyin: Mòqí shì Zhōngguó gǔdài de yí gè fùxìng.
example.english: Mòqí is an ancient Chinese two-character surname.
example.fact: 万俟 is an unusual Chinese surname: the character 万, normally read wàn ('ten thousand'), is pronounced mò only here — a trace of its origins among the Xianbei people who ruled parts of northern China before the Tang dynasty.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渲 describes techniques of washing or spreading color, originally with water-based ink.
宣 (xuān) gives a sound close to 渲's reading xuàn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 画家用淡墨渲染出山间的雾气。
example.pinyin: Huàjiā yòng dàn mò xuànrǎn chū shānjiān de wùqì.
example.english: The painter used light ink washes to render the mist in the mountains.
example.fact: 渲染 (xuànrǎn) is the standard term in Chinese ink painting for building up tone with repeated light washes — a technique similar to what English calls a 'wash' in watercolor painting.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 橄榄 (olive) is the fruit of a tree, so 榄 carries the wood/plant radical.
览 (lǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 榄's reading.

example.hanzi: 地中海地区盛产橄榄。
example.pinyin: Dìzhōnghǎi dìqū shèngchǎn gǎnlǎn.
example.english: The Mediterranean region produces olives abundantly.
example.fact: Some cultivated olive trees in the Mediterranean are estimated to be well over a thousand years old, among the longest-lived fruit trees grown by humans.

etymologyHint: A silk cocoon 艹 spun by a worm 虫

components.note: In the simplified form, 艹 sits atop like a wrapping or covering — likely a simplification of the silk/enclosing element in the traditional 繭, rather than literally 'grass.'
虫 (insect/worm) — the cocoon is spun by a silkworm.

example.hanzi: 蚕在结茧的时候会吐丝。
example.pinyin: Cán zài jié jiǎn de shíhou huì tǔ sī.
example.english: When a silkworm spins its cocoon, it produces silk thread.
example.fact: A single silkworm cocoon is spun from one continuous filament of silk that can run several hundred meters long, sometimes over a kilometer, before it ends.

etymologyHint: The child 兒 of a rain cloud 雨

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霓 names a rainbow-like phenomenon that appears with rain.

兒 (child) sits below the rain — one traditional reading treats a secondary, fainter rainbow (霓) as the 'child' of the main rainbow (虹); 兒's own reading (ér) isn't close to ní, so this is a meaning link, not a sound one.

example.hanzi: 雨后天空同时出现了虹和霓。
example.pinyin: Yǔ hòu tiānkōng tóngshí chūxiàn le hóng hé ní.
example.english: After the rain, both a hóng and a ní rainbow appeared in the sky at once.
example.fact: In classical Chinese, a rainbow was actually described with two separate words: 虹 (hóng) for the bright primary rainbow and 霓 (ní) for the fainter secondary one that sometimes appears above it.

meanings: used in 鸚鵡|鹦鹉[ying1 wu3]

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹉 only appears in 鹦鹉 (yīngwǔ), 'parrot.'
武 (wǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with the second syllable of 鹦鹉.

example.hanzi: 那只鹦鹉会说好几句话。
example.pinyin: Nà zhī yīngwǔ huì shuō hǎo jǐ jù huà.
example.english: That parrot can say several phrases.
example.fact: An African grey parrot named Alex, studied for decades by researcher Irene Pepperberg, learned to use over 100 English words meaningfully, including numbers and shapes.

etymologyHint: A body ⺼ wrapped in cloth 疋

components.note: ⺼ (a form of 肉, flesh) — an early sense of 胥 involved preparing meat, before the character broadened to 'all' and 'mutually.'

example.hanzi: 胥吏在古代衙门里处理文书。
example.pinyin: Xúlì zài gǔdài yámén lǐ chǔlǐ wénshū.
example.english: Clerks (xúlì) handled paperwork in ancient government offices.
example.fact: In imperial China, 胥吏 were low-ranking clerks who ran the day-to-day paperwork of local government — often wielding more real influence than their rank suggested, since they alone understood the bureaucratic procedures.

components.note: 玨 (a form of 王/玉, jade) doesn't mean jade literally here — in 琵琶 the plucking hand motions were likened to jade pieces clicking together, giving the instrument's name its jade-related radical.
巴 (bā) gives a sound close to 琶's reading pá, sharing the same vowel and a related initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 她弹得一手好琵琶。
example.pinyin: Tā tán de yì shǒu hǎo pípá.
example.english: She plays the pípá (lute) beautifully.
example.fact: The pípá is a pear-shaped, four-stringed lute over a thousand years old in China; its name is traditionally said to imitate its two basic plucking motions — pí, forward, and pá, backward.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撬 describes prying or levering something open by hand.
毳 (cuì) is the traditional phonetic element, but its modern reading has moved far from 撬's qiào — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他用撬棍撬开了木箱。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng qiàogùn qiàokāi le mùxiāng.
example.english: He used a crowbar to pry open the wooden box.
example.fact: 撬 is one of many Chinese characters whose 'phonetic' component no longer sounds much like the character itself — roughly two thousand years of sound change have pulled the two readings apart.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 橘 names a citrus tree and its fruit, the mandarin orange.
矞 is the phonetic element from the character's history, though its own reading has drifted from jú over time — the connection today is more etymological than audible.

example.hanzi: 冬天的时候,我喜欢吃橘子。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān de shíhou, wǒ xǐhuan chī júzi.
example.english: In winter, I like to eat mandarin oranges.
example.fact: Mandarin oranges are one of the ancestral citrus species behind many modern hybrids — sweet oranges themselves are believed to be a natural cross between mandarin and pomelo.

components.note: 酉 (wine) — ancient medicine used alcohol both to disinfect wounds and as a solvent for other medicines, so 醫 carries the wine radical.
殹 (yì) gives a sound close to 醫's reading yī, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 中醫已經有幾千年的歷史了。
example.pinyin: Zhōngyī yǐjīng yǒu jǐ qiān nián de lìshǐ le.
example.english: Traditional Chinese medicine already has a history of several thousand years.
example.fact: 醫 is the traditional form of the simplified character 医 ('doctor, medicine'); it survives today mainly in the term 中醫, still the standard spelling for Traditional Chinese Medicine in Taiwan and Hong Kong.

etymologyHint: To divine 占 by hand 扌; 占 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拈 describes picking something up delicately with the fingers.
占 (to divine, to occupy) shares 拈's final -ian rather loosely; the character may originally have pictured fingers plucking at something the way one draws a lot for divination.

example.hanzi: 她随手拈起一片叶子。
example.pinyin: Tā suíshǒu niān qǐ yí piàn yèzi.
example.english: She casually picked up a leaf with her fingers.
example.fact: 拈 appears in the classical idiom 拈花惹草 (niānhuā rěcǎo), literally 'to pick flowers and provoke grass' — a figurative, disapproving way of describing philandering.

meanings: an article made of bamboo strips

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 笆 names fences and baskets woven from bamboo strips.
巴 (bā) gives the sound — an exact match with 笆's reading.

example.hanzi: 村子周围围着竹笆。
example.pinyin: Cūnzi zhōuwéi wéizhe zhú bā.
example.english: A bamboo fence surrounds the village.
example.fact: 笆 almost always appears in the compound 篱笆 (líba), the everyday word for a fence woven from bamboo, twigs, or reeds around a garden or yard.

etymologyHint: Made whole 全 after an illness 疒; 全 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痊 describes recovering from an illness.
全 (whole, complete) — being 'made whole again' is the core image of recovery; 全 is also read quán, exactly matching 痊's own pronunciation.

example.hanzi: 他的病终于痊愈了。
example.pinyin: Tā de bìng zhōngyú quányù le.
example.english: His illness has finally healed completely.
example.fact: 痊 has essentially lost its independent use in modern Mandarin — it now appears almost only in the single compound 痊愈 (quányù), 'to fully recover.'

example.hanzi: 这件事亟待解决。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì jí dài jiějué.
example.english: This matter urgently needs to be resolved.
example.fact: 亟 is a literary character now mostly confined to set phrases like 亟待解决 (jí dài jiějué, 'urgently needs resolving') — everyday speech uses the more common 急 instead.

meanings: name of a river in Shanxi

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渭 names the Wei River.
胃 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 渭's reading.

example.hanzi: 渭河是黄河的一条支流。
example.pinyin: Wèi Hé shì Huáng Hé de yì tiáo zhīliú.
example.english: The Wei River is a tributary of the Yellow River.
example.fact: The Wei River valley, which gives 渭 its name, was the heartland of the ancient Qin state — the base from which the First Emperor unified China in 221 BCE.

components.note: 犭 (a beast, from 犬) — 狙 originally named a kind of ape or monkey.
且, in its less common reading jū, gives the sound — an exact match with 狙's reading.

example.hanzi: 狙击手潜伏在山顶。
example.pinyin: Jūjīshǒu qiánfú zài shāndǐng.
example.english: The sniper lay hidden on the hilltop.
example.fact: 狙击 (jūjī, 'to snipe') borrows its imagery from an animal: 狙 originally meant a kind of ape known for stalking prey stealthily, and the sense of a hidden, patient ambush grew from that image.

etymologyHint: Possibly 可 jade 王; 可 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 王 (a form of 玉, jade) — 珂 names an inferior, jade-like stone, so it borrows the jade radical for its material.
可 (kě) is close in sound to 珂's reading kē, differing only in tone — likely functioning as a sound cue alongside the jade meaning.

example.hanzi: 古人用珂做装饰品。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén yòng kē zuò zhuāngshì pǐn.
example.english: Ancient people used kē-stone to make ornaments.
example.fact: 珂 named a lower grade of jade-like stone, distinct from 玉 (yù), true jade — ancient China graded jade and jade-like stones almost as carefully as gemstones are graded today.

meanings: to peel (with a potato peeler etc)

components.note: 刂 (a form of 刀, knife) — 刨 describes shaving or planing wood with a blade.
包 (bāo) is the phonetic element, sharing 刨's rhyme -ao but differing in initial consonant and tone — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 木匠用刨子刨平木板。
example.pinyin: Mùjiang yòng páozi páo píng mùbǎn.
example.english: The carpenter used a plane to smooth the wooden board flat.
example.fact: 刨 has two common readings that split the same root: bào for the woodworking tool itself, and páo for the action of planing or digging — noun and verb readings drifting apart from one character.

etymologyHint: An insect 虫 changing 兑 its skin; 兑 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蜕 describes an insect shedding its skin during molting.
兑 (duì) is close in sound to 蜕's reading tuì, differing only in the initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 蝉蜕下的壳留在树上。
example.pinyin: Chántuì xià de ké liú zài shùshàng.
example.english: The shell the cicada shed was left behind on the tree.
example.fact: 蜕变 (tuìbiàn), literally 'to molt and transform,' is used figuratively in Chinese for a profound personal or social transformation — much like English uses 'metamorphosis.'

etymologyHint: Elegant 彦 words 讠; 彦 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谚 names a saying passed down in speech, a proverb.
彦 (a learned, accomplished man) shares 谚's exact reading yàn — proverbs were traditionally regarded as the distilled wisdom of such men.

example.hanzi: 这句谚语流传了很多年。
example.pinyin: Zhè jù yànyǔ liúchuán le hěn duō nián.
example.english: This proverb has been passed down for many years.
example.fact: 谚语 (yànyǔ) is the general Chinese word for 'proverb'; the character 谚 itself is now almost never used alone outside this one compound.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 憧 describes an unsettled state of mind: yearning, or wavering indecision.
童 (tóng) shares 憧's rhyme -ong, though the initial consonant and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 年轻人对未来充满憧憬。
example.pinyin: Niánqīng rén duì wèilái chōngmǎn chōngjǐng.
example.english: Young people are full of hopeful anticipation for the future.
example.fact: 憧 survives almost entirely in the compound 憧憬 (chōngjǐng), 'to look forward to, to long for' — a hopeful yearning toward something not yet realized.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 瞟 describes a sidelong glance or look.
票 (piào) gives a sound close to 瞟's reading piǎo, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她瞟了他一眼,没说话。
example.pinyin: Tā piǎo le tā yì yǎn, méi shuōhuà.
example.english: She glanced sideways at him without saying anything.
example.fact: 瞟 specifically describes a quick, sidelong glance, often tinged with disdain or suspicion — distinct from 看 (a plain, direct look) or 盯 (a fixed stare).

meanings: used in 饅頭|馒头[man2 tou5]

components.note: 饣 (food) — 馒头 (steamed bread) is, unsurprisingly, food.
曼 (màn) gives a sound close to 馒's reading mán, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 早饭我喜欢吃馒头。
example.pinyin: Zǎofàn wǒ xǐhuan chī mántou.
example.english: For breakfast I like to eat steamed bread.
example.fact: 馒头 (mántou) is steamed rather than baked — steaming has long been one of the most common ways to cook staple foods in China, while oven-baking spread more widely only later, influenced by Western techniques.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拗 describes bending, twisting, or forcing something by hand.
幼 (yòu) is the phonetic element from the character's older history, but its modern reading has diverged well beyond 拗's ǎo — the link today is more etymological than audible.

example.hanzi: 他用力把树枝拗断了。
example.pinyin: Tā yònglì bǎ shùzhī ǎo duàn le.
example.english: He forcefully bent the branch until it broke.
example.fact: 拗 has three different readings in modern Mandarin depending on its meaning — ǎo (to bend by force), ào (awkward, as in 拗口, 'hard to pronounce'), and niù (stubborn, as in 执拗) — one character doing the work of three unrelated-sounding words.

etymologyHint: A hand 巾 holding a broom with the head 彐 held up

components.note: 帚 is a simplified picture of a hand-broom: bristles at the bottom, bound together and gathered under a handle at the top.

example.hanzi: 她拿着扫帚打扫院子。
example.pinyin: Tā ná zhe sàozhou dǎsǎo yuànzi.
example.english: She swept the courtyard with a broom.
example.fact: 帚 is one of the oldest pictographic characters still in daily use — its shape, a bundle of bristles bound to a handle, has stayed recognizable since its earliest oracle-bone forms more than three thousand years ago.

etymologyHint: A metal 钅 fork 叉; 叉 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) — a 钗 hairpin is a piece of metal jewelry.
叉 (a fork, a forked shape) — traditional hairpins had two forked prongs; 叉's reading chā is also close to 钗's chāi, differing only in the vowel glide.

example.hanzi: 古代女子常用钗来固定发髻。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài nǚzǐ chángyòng chāi lái gùdìng fàjì.
example.english: Ancient women often used ornamental hairpins to hold their hair buns in place.
example.fact: In classical Chinese poetry, breaking a two-pronged hairpin in half — as in Bai Juyi's famous poem Chang Hen Ge — became a symbol of parting lovers, each keeping one half as a token for a hoped-for reunion.

meanings: tearing of paper, ripping of fabric etc

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哧 is an onomatopoeia for sounds made with the mouth or breath, like a giggle or a rip.
赤 (chì) gives a sound close to 哧's reading chī, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她哧的一声笑了出来。
example.pinyin: Tā chī de yì shēng xiào le chūlái.
example.english: She let out a quick laughing sound.
example.fact: 哧 is a pure sound-word with no meaning beyond the sound itself — it can represent a stifled giggle, the hiss of tearing cloth, or a quick exhale, depending on context.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喋 describes chattering or nagging talk.
枼 (yè) is the phonetic element from the character's history, but its modern reading no longer resembles 喋's dié — the link today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 她喋喋不休地讲个不停。
example.pinyin: Tā diédié bùxiū de jiǎng gè bùtíng.
example.english: She chattered on and on without stopping.
example.fact: 喋喋不休 (diédié bùxiū), 'talking endlessly without stopping,' is one of the few places 喋 still appears in modern Mandarin.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — the 箫 is a vertical bamboo flute.
肃 (sù) is the traditional phonetic element, though its modern reading no longer resembles 箫's xiāo — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他吹箫的声音很悠远。
example.pinyin: Tā chuī xiāo de shēngyīn hěn yōuyuǎn.
example.english: The sound of his flute-playing was distant and lingering.
example.fact: The 箫, a vertical end-blown bamboo flute, is one of China's oldest wind instruments — bone flutes of a similar age found at the Jiahu archaeological site date back roughly 8,000 to 9,000 years.

example.hanzi: 他为人刁钻,爱耍花招。
example.pinyin: Tā wéirén diāozuān, ài shuǎ huāzhāo.
example.english: He's a crafty person who likes to play tricks.
example.fact: 刁 is itself the phonetic component in 叼 (diāo, 'to hold in the mouth') — the two characters are written almost identically, differing only by the addition of a mouth radical 口.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 怦 describes the heart pounding, as in excitement or nervousness.
平 (píng) shares 怦's initial consonant and nasal ending, though the vowel and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,他的心怦怦直跳。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā de xīn pēngpēng zhí tiào.
example.english: Hearing this news, his heart pounded rapidly.
example.fact: 怦怦 (pēngpēng) is an onomatopoeia specifically for a fast-beating heart — one of several heartbeat-related sound words in Chinese, alongside the heavier thump of 咚咚 (dōngdōng).

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 缭 describes winding or wrapping thread or fabric around something.
尞 gives the sound — an exact match with 缭's reading liáo, and is the shared root behind a family of liáo-reading characters, including 燎 (to scorch) and 僚 (colleague).

example.hanzi: 山间云雾缭绕。
example.pinyin: Shānjiān yúnwù liáorào.
example.english: Mist swirls and wreathes among the mountains.
example.fact: 缭绕 (liáorào), 'to curl and wind around,' is the standard word for describing mist, smoke, or melody drifting and lingering in the air in Chinese poetry and description.

etymologyHint: Separated 辶 by a border 冋; 冋 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 辶 (to walk, to move) — 迥 describes things set apart or far removed from each other.
冋 (jiōng, an old word for an outlying district) is close in sound to 迥's reading jiǒng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 两人的性格迥然不同。
example.pinyin: Liǎng rén de xìnggé jiǒngrán bùtóng.
example.english: The two people's personalities are utterly different.
example.fact: 迥 survives in modern Mandarin almost entirely through the set phrase 迥然不同 (jiǒngrán bùtóng), 'utterly different' — used to emphasize a stark contrast.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 湄 describes the bank or shore where water meets land.
眉 (méi) gives the sound — an exact match with 湄's reading.

example.hanzi: 他们在江湄散步。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài jiāngméi sànbù.
example.english: They took a walk along the riverbank.
example.fact: 湄 is a literary word for 'riverbank' now largely replaced by 岸 or 边 in everyday speech — it survives mainly in place names and poetic writing, such as the Mekong River's Chinese name 湄公河 (Méigōng Hé).

components.note: 石 (stone) — 磐 names a large, solid rock or boulder.
般 (bān) shares 磐's final -an and a related initial consonant, though the tone differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 这座桥的地基坚如磐石。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò qiáo de dìjī jiān rú pánshí.
example.english: This bridge's foundation is as solid as a rock.
example.fact: 坚如磐石 (jiān rú pánshí), 'solid as a boulder,' is a common Chinese idiom for describing something completely unshakeable, whether a friendship, an alliance, or a physical structure.

meanings: short name for Chongqing 重慶|重庆[Chong2 qing4]

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渝 originally described water changing color or turning turbid; the sense broadened to 'to change' generally.
俞 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 渝's reading.

example.hanzi: 重庆简称渝,是一座山城。
example.pinyin: Chóngqìng jiǎnchēng Yú, shì yí zuò shānchéng.
example.english: Chongqing's short name is 'Yú'; it is a mountain city.
example.fact: 渝 is the official single-character abbreviation for Chongqing, seen on that city's vehicle license plates — each Chinese province-level region has its own such abbreviation.

etymologyHint: A cover-cloth 冖 on a table 几

components.note: 冖 (a covering, a roof) — 冗 pictures someone sheltered indoors.
几 (a small table or stool) sits beneath the roof — the image of someone idly seated indoors gave rise to 冗's sense of being superfluous or idle.

example.hanzi: 这份报告写得太冗长了。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn bàogào xiě de tài rǒngcháng le.
example.english: This report is written far too long-windedly.
example.fact: 冗 pairs with 长 in 冗长 (rǒngcháng, 'tediously long-winded') and with 员 in 冗员 (rǒngyuán, 'redundant staff') — both common criticisms in Chinese office and bureaucratic language.

components.note: 文 carries the meaning role here, though the connection between 'pattern/culture' and 'mourning' isn't very transparent — such old semantic assignments sometimes reflect convention more than clear logic.
门 (mén) shares 闵's initial consonant and nasal final, though the vowel and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 闵是中国的一个姓氏。
example.pinyin: Mǐn shì Zhōngguó de yí gè xìngshì.
example.english: Mǐn is a Chinese surname.
example.fact: 闵 was the given name of Min Ziqian (闵子骞), one of Confucius's most celebrated disciples, praised in the Analects for his filial devotion.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 噶 is used mainly for transliterating foreign sounds, hence the mouth radical for a sound-word.
葛 (gě/gé) shares 噶's initial consonant, though the vowel and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 噶举派是藏传佛教的一个流派。
example.pinyin: Gájǔpài shì Zàngchuán Fójiào de yí gè liúpài.
example.english: The Kagyu school is one lineage of Tibetan Buddhism.
example.fact: 噶 is used almost exclusively to transliterate foreign and Tibetan sounds — it appears in 噶举 (Kagyu, a school of Tibetan Buddhism) and in 噶厦 (Kashag, the former Tibetan governing council).

meanings: (Tw) to adhere; to stick on; to glue

components.note: 黍 (millet, a sticky grain) — 黏 describes stickiness, glueyness.
占 (zhàn/zhān) is the phonetic element from the character's older history, though its modern reading no longer resembles 黏's nián — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 糯米煮熟后会变得很黏。
example.pinyin: Nuòmǐ zhǔ shú hòu huì biàn de hěn nián.
example.english: After glutinous rice is cooked, it becomes very sticky.
example.fact: 黏 and 粘 are near-duplicate characters in modern usage — current mainland standard favors 黏 for describing sticky textures (黏土, 黏膜), while reserving 粘 mostly for the verb 'to stick to' (粘贴).

components.note: 艹 (plant) — one sense of 蕃 is 'luxuriant, flourishing (vegetation).'
番 (fān) gives the sound — an exact match with 蕃's reading.

example.hanzi: 吐蕃是古代青藏高原上的政权。
example.pinyin: Tǔbō shì gǔdài Qīng-Zàng Gāoyuán shàng de zhèngquán.
example.english: Tubo was an ancient state on the Tibetan Plateau.
example.fact: 吐蕃 (Tǔbō) — where 蕃 is read bō rather than fān, an exception — was the Tibetan Empire that rivaled Tang China in the 7th to 9th centuries.

components.note: 弼 depicts a frame with a bow 弓 braced on each side of a center piece — an ancient tool used to straighten a warped bow, which gave the character its extended sense of 'to correct, to assist.'

example.hanzi: 他是国君的辅弼之臣。
example.pinyin: Tā shì guójūn de fǔbì zhī chén.
example.english: He was a minister who assisted and supported the ruler.
example.fact: 弼 appears almost exclusively in 辅弼 (fǔbì), a classical term for a top minister who assists and 'corrects' the ruler — echoing the character's root sense of straightening a bent bow.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驿 names relay stations for dispatching horses and messages along an official route.

example.hanzi: 古代驿站为送信的人提供换马的地方。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài yìzhàn wèi sòngxìn de rén tígōng huànmǎ de dìfang.
example.english: Ancient relay stations provided a place for messengers to change horses.
example.fact: 驿站 (yìzhàn), the network of relay stations along China's imperial roads, could relay urgent messages several hundred kilometers in a single day by handing them off between mounted riders and fresh horses.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淄 names the Zi River in Shandong.
甾 (zī) gives the sound — an exact match with 淄's reading.

example.hanzi: 淄博是山东省的一座城市。
example.pinyin: Zībó shì Shāndōng Shěng de yí zuò chéngshì.
example.english: Zibo is a city in Shandong province.
example.fact: 淄 names the Zi River, which gives the city of Zibo (淄博) — a major center of ancient Qi state culture — half of its name.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饺子 (dumplings) are, of course, food.
交 (jiāo) gives a sound close to 饺's reading jiǎo, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 过年的时候,一家人一起包饺子。
example.pinyin: Guònián de shíhou, yì jiā rén yìqǐ bāo jiǎozi.
example.english: During the Spring Festival, the whole family makes dumplings together.
example.fact: In northern China, eating jiǎozi at midnight on Lunar New Year's Eve is a long-standing tradition — their crescent shape is said to resemble old silver ingots, symbolizing wealth for the coming year.

etymologyHint: To sit 居 on one's feet 足; 居 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踞 describes crouching or sitting back on one's haunches.
居 (to reside, to sit) is close in sound to 踞's reading jù, differing only in tone, and reinforces the sense of settling down or occupying a position.

example.hanzi: 老虎盘踞在山头。
example.pinyin: Lǎohǔ pánjù zài shāntóu.
example.english: The tiger crouches, dominating the hilltop.
example.fact: 盘踞 (pánjù), 'to occupy and dominate,' often describes bandits, warlords, or wild animals holding a strategic position — the crouching posture of 踞 evokes controlling a place by force.

components.note: 韦 (leather, hide) — a 韬 is a leather sheath or bow-case.
舀 (yǎo) is the phonetic element from the character's history, but its modern reading no longer resembles 韬's tāo — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他胸怀韬略,深藏不露。
example.pinyin: Tā xiōnghuái tāolüè, shēn cáng bú lù.
example.english: He harbors deep strategy, keeping it well hidden.
example.fact: 韬 appears in 韬略 (tāolüè, 'military strategy') and in the idiom 韬光养晦 (tāoguāng-yǎnghuì), 'to conceal one's strength and bide one's time' — a concept with deep roots in Chinese strategic thought.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婷 is used only in names and compounds describing feminine grace.
亭 (tíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 婷's reading.

example.hanzi: 婷婷是个很受欢迎的名字。
example.pinyin: Tíngtíng shì gè hěn shòu huānyíng de míngzi.
example.english: Tingting is a very popular given name.
example.fact: 婷 exists almost solely as a name character — it carries no independent meaning beyond 'graceful, pretty,' and appears mostly in given names like 婷婷 or 雅婷.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 唆 describes inciting someone through talk.
夋 is the shared phonetic root behind several modern readings — suō here, but jùn in related characters like 竣 and 浚 — centuries of sound change have pulled these apart from a common origin.

example.hanzi: 他唆使朋友做坏事。
example.pinyin: Tā suōshǐ péngyou zuò huàishì.
example.english: He incited his friend to do something bad.
example.fact: 唆 almost always appears in 唆使 (suōshǐ), 'to incite, to instigate' — a word with a clearly negative connotation, unlike neutral verbs of persuasion.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蜒 describes crawling creatures like millipedes and slugs.
延 (yán) gives the sound — an exact match with 蜒's reading.

example.hanzi: 蜿蜒的小路通向山顶。
example.pinyin: Wānyán de xiǎolù tōngxiàng shāndǐng.
example.english: The winding path leads to the mountaintop.
example.fact: 蜒 survives almost entirely in 蜿蜒 (wānyán), 'winding, meandering,' used to describe everything from mountain paths to rivers to dragons in Chinese art and writing.

etymologyHint: To cling to someone 亻 in fear 畏; 畏 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (a person) — 偎 describes people cuddling or nestling close together.
畏 (wèi) is close in sound to 偎's reading wēi, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 孩子偎在妈妈的怀里睡着了。
example.pinyin: Háizi wēi zài māma de huáilǐ shuìzháo le.
example.english: The child nestled against her mother's chest and fell asleep.
example.fact: 偎 typically describes an affectionate, protective closeness — as in 依偎 (yīwēi), 'to snuggle up to someone' — rather than mere physical proximity.

components.note: 木 (tree) — early presses for extracting oil or juice were built from wood.
窄 (zhǎi) shares 榨's initial consonant, though the final and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 工人用机器榨取花生油。
example.pinyin: Gōngrén yòng jīqì zhàqǔ huāshēngyóu.
example.english: Workers use machines to press out peanut oil.
example.fact: 榨 gives its name to 压榨 (yāzhà), literally 'to press and squeeze,' which is also used figuratively for exploiting or squeezing value out of workers or resources.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漉 describes straining or filtering liquid.
鹿 (lù) gives the sound — an exact match with 漉's reading.

example.hanzi: 他用纱布把豆浆漉干净。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng shābù bǎ dòujiāng lù gānjìng.
example.english: He used gauze to strain the soy milk clean.
example.fact: 漉 is a fairly literary character today; the everyday verb for 'to strain, to filter' in most contexts is now the modern compound 过滤 (guòlǜ).

components.note: 石 (stone) — a 碉 is a stone watchtower or blockhouse.
周 (zhōu) is the phonetic element from the character's history, though its modern reading no longer resembles 碉's diāo — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 山上有一座古老的碉楼。
example.pinyin: Shān shàng yǒu yí zuò gǔlǎo de diāolóu.
example.english: There is an old stone watchtower on the mountain.
example.fact: 碉楼 (diāolóu), fortified stone watchtowers, are especially associated with the Qiang and Tibetan communities of western Sichuan, some standing for centuries as both homes and defensive structures.

components.note: 皈 is essentially a specialized variant of 归 (guī, 'to return'), coined for Buddhist use — 反 (to turn back) with 白 (white, often linked to purity or clarity) evokes turning back toward a state of spiritual clarity.

example.hanzi: 他决定皈依佛教。
example.pinyin: Tā juédìng guīyī Fójiào.
example.english: He decided to convert to (take refuge in) Buddhism.
example.fact: 皈依 (guīyī) is the standard Buddhist term for taking refuge in the Three Jewels — the Buddha, the teachings, and the monastic community — marking a formal conversion or recommitment to the faith.

components.note: 矛 (spear) — 矜 originally named the shaft or handle of a spear; the senses of 'pity' and 'boastful' developed later.
今 (jīn) gives the sound — an exact match with 矜's reading.

example.hanzi: 他从不矜夸自己的成就。
example.pinyin: Tā cóngbù jīnkuā zìjǐ de chéngjiù.
example.english: He never boasts about his own achievements.
example.fact: 矜 carries two nearly opposite senses depending on context: 'to pity, to sympathize with' (as in 矜恤) and 'to boast, to be conceited' (as in 骄矜) — both grew from an original sense tied to holding oneself with a certain bearing.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — a 笈 was a bamboo box or basket for carrying books.
及 (jí) gives the sound — an exact match with 笈's reading.

example.hanzi: 古代学子常常负笈求学。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài xuézǐ chángcháng fùjí qiúxué.
example.english: Ancient students often traveled far, carrying their books on their backs, to seek an education.
example.fact: 负笈 (fùjí), literally 'carrying a book-case on one's back,' is a classical Chinese expression for traveling away from home to study.

components.note: 木 (wood) — a 枷 was a wooden yoke or cangue locked around a prisoner's neck.
加 (jiā) gives the sound — an exact match with 枷's reading.

example.hanzi: 犯人的脖子上戴着木枷。
example.pinyin: Fànrén de bózi shàng dàizhe mù jiā.
example.english: The prisoner wore a wooden yoke around his neck.
example.fact: The cangue (枷), a heavy wooden collar-like restraint, was a common form of public punishment in imperial China, forcing the wearer to display their crime while unable to feed or care for themselves easily.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲨 names sharks.
沙 (shā) gives the sound — an exact match with 鲨's reading.

example.hanzi: 大白鲨是海洋中最大的掠食性鱼类之一。
example.pinyin: Dàbáishā shì hǎiyáng zhōng zuìdà de lüèshíxìng yúlèi zhī yī.
example.english: The great white shark is one of the largest predatory fish in the ocean.
example.fact: Sharks have existed for over 400 million years, predating dinosaurs by roughly 200 million years and surviving multiple mass extinctions.

etymologyHint: To walk 足 quietly 聂; 聂 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹑 describes stepping softly or quietly, as when tiptoeing.
聂 shares 蹑's exact reading niè, functioning as the sound cue for this character.

example.hanzi: 他蹑手蹑脚地走进房间。
example.pinyin: Tā nièshǒu-nièjiǎo de zǒujìn fángjiān.
example.english: He crept into the room, moving quietly on tiptoe.
example.fact: 蹑手蹑脚 (nièshǒu-nièjiǎo), 'creeping on tiptoe,' is the standard Chinese phrase for moving stealthily and quietly, often used for sneaking around without waking someone.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 瀚 describes vastness, especially of water or open space.
翰 (hàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 瀚's reading.

example.hanzi: 浩瀚的沙漠一望无际。
example.pinyin: Hàohàn de shāmò yíwàng-wújì.
example.english: The vast desert stretches endlessly to the horizon.
example.fact: 瀚 appears almost always in 浩瀚 (hàohàn), 'vast, boundless' — a word used for deserts, oceans, and even the vastness of outer space or historical records.

components.note: 酉 (originally 'wine jar,' broadened to fermented foods) — 酪 names fermented dairy products like cheese and koumiss.
各 (gè) is the phonetic element from the character's history, but its modern reading no longer resembles 酪's lào — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 她很喜欢吃奶酪。
example.pinyin: Tā hěn xǐhuan chī nǎilào.
example.english: She really likes eating cheese.
example.fact: 酪 covers a range of fermented milk products in Chinese history — from 奶酪 (cheese) to 马奶酪 (koumiss) — reflecting dairy-herding influences from the nomadic peoples of the northern steppe.

etymologyHint: To use cruel 虐 words 讠; 虐 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谑 describes joking, teasing speech.
虐 (nüè) shares 谑's rhyme -üe, though the initial consonant differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 朋友之间开点玩笑,谑而不虐。
example.pinyin: Péngyou zhījiān kāi diǎn wánxiào, xuè ér bú nüè.
example.english: Among friends, a little joking is fine — teasing without cruelty.
example.fact: 谑而不虐 (xuè ér bú nüè), 'teasing without being cruel,' traces back to a line in the classical anthology Shijing (Book of Songs) describing good-natured banter that stops short of hurting anyone.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 癖 originally described an internal ailment, later broadening to any deep-seated habit or craving.
辟 (pì) gives a sound close to 癖's reading pǐ, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他有收集老照片的癖好。
example.pinyin: Tā yǒu shōují lǎo zhàopiàn de pǐhào.
example.english: He has a hobby (quirky habit) of collecting old photographs.
example.fact: 癖好 (pǐhào), 'a personal quirk or hobby,' still carries a trace of 癖's original medical sense — the character's oldest meaning was an actual physical ailment, a lump or blockage in the abdomen.

etymologyHint: A used up 尽 fire 火; 尽 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 火 (fire) — 烬 names the ashes and cinders left after a fire burns out.
尽 (used up, exhausted) shares 烬's exact reading jìn — fittingly, since ash is what's left when fire has used everything up.

example.hanzi: 大火过后,只剩下一片灰烬。
example.pinyin: Dàhuǒ guòhòu, zhǐ shèngxià yí piàn huījìn.
example.english: After the great fire, only a stretch of ashes remained.
example.fact: 灰烬 (huījìn), 'ashes,' is often used figuratively in Chinese for something utterly destroyed or a plan reduced to nothing — much like the English phrase 'burned to ashes.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 揩 describes wiping or rubbing something clean with the hand.
皆 (jiē) is the phonetic element from the character's history, but its modern reading no longer resembles 揩's kāi — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他拿毛巾揩干了脸上的水。
example.pinyin: Tā ná máojīn kāi gān le liǎn shàng de shuǐ.
example.english: He used a towel to wipe the water off his face dry.
example.fact: 揩 survives mainly in southern Mandarin and dialect-influenced speech; across most of the north, 擦 (cā) is the everyday word for 'to wipe.'

components.note: 火 (fire) — 炙 pictures meat being roasted over a fire.
月 here is a form of 肉 (meat), not a sound-clue — despite being tagged phonetic, its reading yuè bears no resemblance to zhì, and the character is best understood as picturing meat held above fire.

example.hanzi: 烈日下,大地像被炙烤一样。
example.pinyin: Lièrì xià, dàdì xiàng bèi zhìkǎo yíyàng.
example.english: Under the scorching sun, the ground seemed to be roasting.
example.fact: 炙 originally pictured a piece of meat held directly over a flame — the character is essentially a tiny illustration of an ancient barbecue, later extended to mean any intense, scorching heat.

etymologyHint: To curl up 卷 like a worm 虫; 卷 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 虫 (a worm/insect) — 蜷 describes curling up like a worm.
卷 (juǎn, to curl, to roll up) is close in sound to 蜷's reading quán, sharing the same final and a related initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 小猫蜷缩在沙发上睡觉。
example.pinyin: Xiǎomāo quánsuō zài shāfā shàng shuìjiào.
example.english: The little cat curled up on the sofa to sleep.
example.fact: 蜷缩 (quánsuō), 'to curl up,' describes animals and people drawing their limbs in close to the body — a posture that helps minimize heat loss in cold conditions.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 侏 describes a small or dwarfed person.
朱 (zhū) gives the sound — an exact match with 侏's reading.

example.hanzi: 侏儒症是一种罕见的生长障碍。
example.pinyin: Zhūrúzhèng shì yì zhǒng hǎnjiàn de shēngzhǎng zhàng'ài.
example.english: Dwarfism is a rare growth disorder.
example.fact: 侏 appears almost only in 侏儒 (zhūrú, 'dwarf') and, through a modern loan-coinage, in 侏罗纪 (Zhūluójì), the Chinese name for the Jurassic period — a phonetic transliteration of 'Jura,' unrelated to the character's original meaning.

components.note: 冫 (ice) — 凋 originally linked withering to the cold; the sense of 'wilted, withered' extended from there.
周 (zhōu) is the phonetic element from the character's history, but its modern reading no longer resembles 凋's diāo — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 秋天来了,花草渐渐凋零。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān lái le, huācǎo jiànjiàn diāolíng.
example.english: Autumn has arrived, and the flowers and grass are gradually withering.
example.fact: 凋零 (diāolíng), 'to wither and fall,' is often used figuratively in Chinese poetry and prose for the decline of a family, a dynasty, or a person's fortunes — not just plants.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漪 describes ripples on water.
猗 (yī) gives the sound — an exact match with 漪's reading.

example.hanzi: 湖面漾起一圈圈漪纹。
example.pinyin: Húmiàn yàng qǐ yì quān quān yīwén.
example.english: Ripple after ripple spread across the lake's surface.
example.fact: 漪 is a literary word for ripples, largely replaced in everyday speech by 波纹 (bōwén); today it survives mainly in poetic or descriptive writing.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 悻 describes a feeling of anger or resentment.
幸 (xìng) gives the sound — an exact match with 悻's reading.

example.hanzi: 他悻悻地离开了会议室。
example.pinyin: Tā xìngxìng de líkāi le huìyìshì.
example.english: He left the meeting room in a huff, visibly resentful.
example.fact: 悻悻 (xìngxìng) specifically describes the sulky, resentful manner of someone leaving after being slighted or losing an argument — a very particular shade of anger.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹋 describes stepping or treading on something; it's essentially a variant of 踏.
日 is tagged as the phonetic element here, but rì bears no real resemblance to 蹋's reading tà — the connection, if any, is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 不要糟蹋这么好的食物。
example.pinyin: Búyào zāotà zhème hǎo de shíwù.
example.english: Don't waste such good food.
example.fact: 蹋 today survives almost entirely in 糟蹋 (zāotà), 'to waste, to ruin, to abuse' — used for wasting food, mistreating people, or ruining opportunities alike.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 讪 describes mocking or slandering speech.
山 (shān) gives a sound close to 讪's reading shàn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他被人讪笑,觉得很尴尬。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi rén shànxiào, juéde hěn gāngà.
example.english: He was mocked by others and felt very embarrassed.
example.fact: 讪笑 (shànxiào), 'to mock, to sneer at,' combines 讪 with the common verb 笑 (to laugh) to describe laughing at someone in a scornful way.

meanings: to twitch; to have a spasm

components.note: 扌 (hand) — the hand radical is used broadly here for bodily movement, as in muscle twitching.
畜 (chù) gives the sound — an exact match with 搐's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的手指不停地抽搐。
example.pinyin: Tā de shǒuzhǐ bùtíng de chōuchù.
example.english: His fingers kept twitching uncontrollably.
example.fact: 抽搐 (chōuchù), 'to twitch, to convulse,' is standard medical vocabulary in Chinese for describing muscle spasms and convulsions, including seizures.

components.note: 石 (stone/mineral) — 碘 names iodine, classified along with other mineral elements.
典 (diǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 碘's reading.

example.hanzi: 海带含有丰富的碘。
example.pinyin: Hǎidài hányǒu fēngfù de diǎn.
example.english: Kelp contains abundant iodine.
example.fact: Iodine deficiency was historically a major cause of goiter in inland regions far from the sea — a problem largely solved in many countries by iodizing table salt.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — 帛 names silk fabric.
白 (bái) shares 帛's initial consonant and tone, though the vowel differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 古人在竹简和丝帛上写字。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén zài zhújiǎn hé sī bó shàng xiězì.
example.english: Ancient people wrote on bamboo slips and silk fabric.
example.fact: Before paper became widespread, silk (帛) was one of the main writing surfaces in ancient China — documents written on silk have been recovered from tombs like the Mawangdui site, preserved for over two thousand years.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诠 describes explaining or expounding on something through words.
全 (quán) gives the sound — an exact match with 诠's reading.

example.hanzi: 这本书对经典理论做了详细的诠释。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū duì jīngdiǎn lǐlùn zuò le xiángxì de quánshì.
example.english: This book gives a detailed interpretation of the classic theory.
example.fact: 诠释 (quánshì), 'to interpret, to explain,' is the standard academic term in Chinese for hermeneutics — the theory and practice of interpreting texts.

components.note: 石 (stone) — a 碾 is a stone roller used for grinding grain.
展 (zhǎn) shares 碾's final -an and tone, though the initial consonant differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 农民用石碾把稻谷碾成米。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng shí niǎn bǎ dàogǔ niǎn chéng mǐ.
example.english: Farmers use a stone roller to grind rice grain into rice.
example.fact: The stone roller mill (石碾), turned by animal or human power, was one of the most common grain-processing tools across rural China for centuries before mechanized milling took over.

meanings: grind with a mortar and pestle
(bound form) platform for a martial art contest

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 擂 describes grinding or pounding by hand, as with a mortar and pestle.
雷 (léi) gives the sound — an exact match with 擂's reading.

example.hanzi: 他们在擂台上比武。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài léitái shàng bǐwǔ.
example.english: They compete in martial arts on the fighting platform.
example.fact: 擂台 (léitái) names the raised platform used for martial arts contests and public challenges — the phrase 打擂台 ('to fight on the platform') is still used figuratively for openly challenging a rival or champion in any field.

components.note: 艹 (plant/grass) is reused here mostly for phonetic and categorical convenience — 苯 (benzene) has no real connection to plants despite the radical.
本 (běn) gives the sound — an exact match with 苯's reading.

example.hanzi: 苯是一种重要的有机化合物。
example.pinyin: Běn shì yì zhǒng zhòngyào de yǒujī huàhéwù.
example.english: Benzene is an important organic compound.
example.fact: 苯 (benzene) is a purpose-built character, coined as a sound-alike for the Western scientific name — many 19th- and 20th-century Chinese chemistry terms were created this way, pairing an existing radical with a phonetic match.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诃 describes scolding or rebuking someone verbally.
可 (kě) shares 诃's vowel, though the initial consonant and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 长辈严厉地诃责了他。
example.pinyin: Zhǎngbèi yánlì de hēzé le tā.
example.english: The elder sternly scolded him.
example.fact: 诃 is largely a literary character today, mostly replaced in everyday speech by 呵斥 (hēchì) or simply 骂 (mà) for 'to scold.'

components.note: 钅 (metal) — a 铎 was a large bronze bell used ceremonially or as a military signal.

example.hanzi: 古代的铎声用来传达号令。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài de duó shēng yòng lái chuándá hàolìng.
example.english: The sound of ancient bronze bells was used to convey military orders and commands.
example.fact: 木铎 ('wooden-tongued bell'), a bell with a wooden clapper, was rung by officials to announce new laws to the public in ancient China — the Analects even likens Confucius himself to a 木铎 spreading moral teaching.

components.note: 戊 is thought to picture an ancient broad-bladed weapon similar to 戈 — its use today as the fifth of the Ten Heavenly Stems is a phonetic loan, unrelated to that original weapon meaning.

example.hanzi: 戊戌变法发生在1898年。
example.pinyin: Wùxū Biànfǎ fāshēng zài yī bā jiǔ bā nián.
example.english: The Wuxu Reform took place in 1898.
example.fact: The Ten Heavenly Stems, including 戊, combine with the Twelve Earthly Branches to form the 60-year cycle traditionally used to name years in China — 1898's 戊戌 gave the failed reform movement of that year its name.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 荀 was originally a plant name, later used mainly as a surname.
旬 (xún) gives the sound — an exact match with 荀's reading.

example.hanzi: 荀子是战国时期著名的思想家。
example.pinyin: Xúnzǐ shì Zhànguó shíqī zhùmíng de sīxiǎngjiā.
example.english: Xunzi was a famous thinker of the Warring States period.
example.fact: The philosopher Xunzi notably argued that human nature is originally bad and must be improved through education and ritual — a striking contrast to Mencius's view that human nature is fundamentally good.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驹 names a young horse, a colt or foal.
句 (jù) gives a sound close to 驹's reading jū, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 小马驹在草地上奔跑。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo mǎjū zài cǎodì shàng bēnpǎo.
example.english: The little foal runs on the grassland.
example.fact: 驹 appears in the classical idiom 白驹过隙 (báijū-guòxì), 'a white colt glimpsed through a gap,' a metaphor from the philosopher Zhuangzi for how swiftly life passes.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 攫 describes snatching or seizing something forcefully.
矍 (jué) gives the sound — an exact match with 攫's reading.

example.hanzi: 老鹰俯冲下来,攫住了一只野兔。
example.pinyin: Lǎoyīng fǔchōng xiàlái, juézhù le yì zhī yětù.
example.english: The eagle swooped down and seized a wild hare.
example.fact: 攫取 (juéqǔ), 'to seize, to grab,' often carries a negative connotation in modern Chinese, describing the forceful or illegitimate grabbing of power, profit, or resources.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — 憬 describes a mental awakening or a hopeful vision of the future.
景 (jǐng) gives the sound — an exact match with 憬's reading.

example.hanzi: 他对未来充满憧憬。
example.pinyin: Tā duì wèilái chōngmǎn chōngjǐng.
example.english: He is full of hopeful anticipation for the future.
example.fact: 憬 exists in modern Mandarin almost exclusively within the compound 憧憬 (chōngjǐng), 'to look forward to' — neither half of the compound is commonly used alone.

meanings: to choke on a piece of food

components.note: 口 (mouth/throat) — 哽 describes choking on food or being choked up with emotion.
更 (gèng) gives a sound close to 哽's reading gěng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 说到伤心事,她哽咽了。
example.pinyin: Shuōdào shāngxīn shì, tā gěngyè le.
example.english: Speaking of the sad matter, her voice choked with emotion.
example.fact: 哽咽 (gěngyè), 'to choke up, to sob with a lump in one's throat,' describes the physical sensation of being too emotional to speak clearly.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踵 names the heel.
重 (zhòng) gives a sound close to 踵's reading zhǒng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他接踵而来的问题让人应付不暇。
example.pinyin: Tā jiēzhǒng ér lái de wèntí ràng rén yìngfù bùxiá.
example.english: His problems came one after another, too fast to handle.
example.fact: 接踵而来 (jiēzhǒng-érlái), literally 'arriving heel to heel,' describes things happening one right after another, evoking a crowd of people packed so closely their heels touch.

components.note: 虫 (a small creature, broadened to reptiles) — 蟒 names large constrictor snakes like pythons.
莽 (mǎng) gives the sound — an exact match with 蟒's reading.

example.hanzi: 缅甸蟒是世界上最大的蛇类之一。
example.pinyin: Miǎndiàn Mǎng shì shìjiè shàng zuìdà de shélèi zhī yī.
example.english: The Burmese python is one of the largest snakes in the world.
example.fact: Pythons kill their prey by constriction rather than venom — they wrap around the animal and tighten with each breath it exhales, rather than crushing it in one motion.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漾 describes water rippling or overflowing gently.
羕 (yàng) gives the sound — an exact match with 漾's reading.

example.hanzi: 微风吹过,水面荡漾起波纹。
example.pinyin: Wēifēng chuīguò, shuǐmiàn dàngyàng qǐ bōwén.
example.english: A gentle breeze blew past, and ripples rocked across the water's surface.
example.fact: 荡漾 (dàngyàng), 'to ripple, to sway gently,' is a favorite word in Chinese lyric poetry for describing both rippling water and a heart stirred by emotion.

meanings: to attempt to (find an opportunity to) speak

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 啧 is an onomatopoeia for a clicking-tongue sound made with the mouth.
责 (zé) gives the sound — an exact match with 啧's reading.

example.hanzi: 大家看到这幅画都啧啧称奇。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā kàndào zhè fú huà dōu zézé chēngqí.
example.english: Everyone who saw the painting clicked their tongues in amazement.
example.fact: 啧啧 (zézé) mimics the sound of clicking one's tongue against the roof of the mouth — a sound Chinese speakers make to express admiration or, in a different tone, disapproval.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吮 describes sucking with the mouth.
允 (yǔn) shares 吮's final and tone, though the initial consonant differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 婴儿吮吸着奶瓶。
example.pinyin: Yīng'ér shǔnxī zhe nǎipíng.
example.english: The baby is sucking on the bottle.
example.fact: 吮吸 (shǔnxī), 'to suck,' describes one of the earliest reflexes present in human infants — the sucking reflex is already active before birth and can be observed in the womb by ultrasound.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 楠 names nanmu, a valuable hardwood tree.
南 (nán) gives the sound — an exact match with 楠's reading.

example.hanzi: 金丝楠木是一种非常珍贵的木材。
example.pinyin: Jīnsī nánmù shì yì zhǒng fēicháng zhēnguì de mùcái.
example.english: Golden-thread nanmu is an extremely precious type of wood.
example.fact: Golden-thread nanmu (金丝楠木) was historically reserved for imperial construction and furniture in China, used in parts of the Forbidden City's halls and in imperial coffins.

components.note: 气 (gas) — 氟 names fluorine, a gaseous chemical element.
弗 (fú) gives the sound — an exact match with 氟's reading.

example.hanzi: 很多牙膏里含有氟。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō yágāo lǐ hányǒu fú.
example.english: Many toothpastes contain fluoride.
example.fact: Fluoride is added to toothpaste and some water supplies because it helps rebuild tooth enamel and resist decay — one of the most studied public-health interventions of the 20th century.

meanings: used in 慫恿|怂恿[song3 yong3]

components.note: 心 (heart) — 怂 describes a state of mind: being timid, or urging someone on.
从 (cóng) shares 怂's rhyme -ong and a related initial consonant, though the tone differs — a fairly close, if not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 他怂恿朋友一起去冒险。
example.pinyin: Tā sǒngyǒng péngyou yìqǐ qù màoxiǎn.
example.english: He egged his friend on to go on an adventure together.
example.fact: 怂恿 (sǒngyǒng), 'to incite, to egg on,' almost always describes pushing someone toward a risky or ill-advised action — rarely used for encouraging something sensible.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 叼 describes holding something in the mouth, as a dog holds a bone.
刁 (diāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 叼's reading.

example.hanzi: 小狗嘴里叼着一根骨头。
example.pinyin: Xiǎogǒu zuǐ lǐ diāo zhe yì gēn gǔtou.
example.english: The puppy is holding a bone in its mouth.
example.fact: 叼 is one of the simplest possible phono-semantic characters: it is literally its phonetic component 刁 with a mouth radical 口 added, and nothing else changes.

components.note: 立 (to stand) — 竣 describes a project standing complete, finished.
夋 gives the sound — an exact match with 竣's reading jùn, part of the same phonetic family as 浚.

example.hanzi: 这座大桥终于竣工了。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò dàqiáo zhōngyú jùngōng le.
example.english: This bridge has finally been completed.
example.fact: 竣 survives in modern Mandarin almost entirely in 竣工 (jùngōng), 'to complete construction' — a term seen constantly on Chinese construction-site signage announcing project completion dates.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 偕 describes people doing something together.
皆 (jiē) shares 偕's final -ie, though the initial consonant and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 夫妻二人偕老,携手一生。
example.pinyin: Fūqī èr rén xiélǎo, xiéshǒu yìshēng.
example.english: The husband and wife grow old together, hand in hand for life.
example.fact: 偕 survives mainly in the blessing 白头偕老 (báitóu xiélǎo), 'to grow old together with heads turned white' — a traditional wish offered to newlyweds at Chinese weddings.

etymologyHint: Swirling 旋 water 氵; 旋 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漩 describes swirling water, an eddy or whirlpool.
旋 (to spin, to revolve) shares 漩's exact reading xuán — its meaning of spinning also reinforces the swirling image.

example.hanzi: 河水在这里形成了一个漩涡。
example.pinyin: Héshuǐ zài zhèlǐ xíngchéng le yí gè xuánwō.
example.english: The river water forms a whirlpool here.
example.fact: 漩涡 (xuánwō), 'whirlpool, vortex,' is also used figuratively in Chinese for being caught up in a dangerous or overwhelming situation.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹭 describes shuffling, rubbing against something while moving slowly.
曾 (céng) gives a sound close to 蹭's reading cèng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他蹭着墙边慢慢走过去。
example.pinyin: Tā cèng zhe qiáng biān mànmàn zǒu guòqù.
example.english: He shuffled slowly along, brushing against the wall.
example.fact: 蹭 has picked up a modern slang sense in recent decades: 蹭网 (cèng wǎng), 'to freeload off someone else's Wi-Fi,' extending the old idea of 'rubbing against' something to getting something for free.

example.hanzi: 翌日,他们启程前往北京。
example.pinyin: Yìrì, tāmen qǐchéng qiánwǎng Běijīng.
example.english: The next day, they set off for Beijing.
example.fact: 翌 is a formal, literary word for 'the next day,' used in written narration and news reports; everyday spoken Chinese uses 第二天 instead.

etymologyHint: The part of the body ⺼ that feels 意; 意 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 臆 originally named the chest, before extending to inner feelings and subjective guesses.
意 (thought, idea) shares 臆's exact reading yì, and its meaning reinforces 臆's sense of an inward, subjective thought.

example.hanzi: 这只是他的臆测,并没有证据。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǐshì tā de yìcè, bìng méiyǒu zhèngjù.
example.english: This is just his conjecture, with no evidence at all.
example.fact: 臆测 (yìcè) and 臆断 (yìduàn) both describe judging something based on subjective guesswork rather than facts — 臆 always carries a slightly critical undertone of unfounded assumption.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 挝 describes striking or beating with the hand.
过 (guò) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 挝's wō — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 老挝是东南亚的一个内陆国家。
example.pinyin: Lǎowō shì Dōngnányà de yí gè nèilù guójiā.
example.english: Laos is a landlocked country in Southeast Asia.
example.fact: 挝 is mostly known today for its role in 老挝 (Lǎowō), the Chinese name for Laos — a purely phonetic transliteration unrelated to the character's original meaning of 'to strike.'

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 绚 describes something as brilliantly colorful, like richly patterned silk.
旬 (xún) shares 绚's initial consonant, though the vowel and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 烟花在夜空中绚丽绽放。
example.pinyin: Yānhuā zài yèkōng zhōng xuànlì zhànfàng.
example.english: Fireworks bloom brilliantly in the night sky.
example.fact: 绚丽 (xuànlì), 'brilliantly colorful, dazzling,' is a favorite word in Chinese for describing fireworks, sunsets, and elaborate stage performances.

example.hanzi: 母猫叫唤着,寻找她的猫崽子。
example.pinyin: Mǔmāo jiàohuan zhe, xúnzhǎo tā de māo zǎizi.
example.english: The mother cat calls out, searching for her kittens.
example.fact: 崽 is common in southern Mandarin and dialect-flavored speech for 'offspring' or 'young animal,' as in 猫崽子 (kitten) — it often carries a rough, informal, sometimes affectionate tone, rather like English 'brat' used fondly.

components.note: 米 (rice) — 糜 describes rice or grain cooked down into a thin gruel or porridge.
麻 (má) shares 糜's initial consonant, though the vowel and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 生病的时候,他只能喝点米糜。
example.pinyin: Shēngbìng de shíhou, tā zhǐ néng hē diǎn mǐ mí.
example.english: When he was sick, he could only drink a bit of rice gruel.
example.fact: 糜烂 (mílàn), literally 'gruel-rotten,' is used in Chinese both medically for tissue erosion or ulceration and figuratively for a decadent, corrupted lifestyle.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 瘢 names a scar left after a wound heals.
般 (bān) gives the sound — an exact match with 瘢's reading.

example.hanzi: 他手臂上留下了一道瘢痕。
example.pinyin: Tā shǒubì shàng liúxià le yí dào bānhén.
example.english: A scar was left on his arm.
example.fact: 瘢痕 (bānhén), 'scar,' is the standard medical term in Chinese, distinct from the more everyday 疤 (bā), though the two overlap heavily in casual speech.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跤 describes stumbling, falling, or wrestling — all involving the feet and legs.
交 (jiāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 跤's reading.

example.hanzi: 他不小心摔了一跤。
example.pinyin: Tā bù xiǎoxīn shuāi le yì jiāo.
example.english: He accidentally took a fall.
example.fact: 摔跤 (shuāijiāo) means both 'to fall down' and, as a set term, 'wrestling' — Chinese folk wrestling has its own regional styles distinct from Western freestyle or Greco-Roman wrestling.

components.note: 门 (door) — 阑 originally named a screen or railing set up near a door or entrance.
柬 (jiǎn) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 阑's lán — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 夜已经阑珊,他还没有睡意。
example.pinyin: Yè yǐjīng lánshān, tā hái méiyǒu shuìyì.
example.english: The night had already grown late, yet he still felt no urge to sleep.
example.fact: 阑 survives mainly in literary compounds like 夜阑 ('deep night') and 阑珊 ('waning, fading') — words that evoke something drawing to a quiet, spent close.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 恬 describes a calm, tranquil state of mind.
舌 (shé) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears no real resemblance to 恬's tián — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 退休以后,他过着恬静的生活。
example.pinyin: Tuìxiū yǐhòu, tā guò zhe tiánjìng de shēnghuó.
example.english: After retiring, he lives a peaceful, tranquil life.
example.fact: 恬 pairs with 淡 in 恬淡 ('placid, unconcerned with worldly gain') — an ideal closely tied to the Daoist value of contentment through simplicity and detachment from ambition.

components.note: 豕 (pig) — 豢 describes raising and feeding domestic animals, especially pigs.
龹 is the phonetic element tagged here; it's a rare component whose own reading isn't well established, so the sound link to 豢's huàn is best treated as historical rather than a clear match.

example.hanzi: 农民在家里豢养了几只猪。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín zài jiālǐ huànyǎng le jǐ zhī zhū.
example.english: The farmer raises a few pigs at home.
example.fact: 豢养 (huànyǎng), 'to raise domestic animals,' is sometimes used disapprovingly and figuratively in Chinese for one person supporting and controlling another, much like the English idiom 'to keep someone on a leash.'

meanings: Wen River in northwest Sichuan (same as 汶川)

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汶 names rivers, including the Wen River in Shandong and Sichuan.
文 (wén) gives a sound close to 汶's reading wèn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 汶川地震发生在2008年。
example.pinyin: Wènchuān Dìzhèn fāshēng zài èr líng líng bā nián.
example.english: The Wenchuan earthquake occurred in 2008.
example.fact: 汶川, the Sichuan county whose name uses this character, became internationally known after the devastating magnitude-8.0 earthquake that struck there on May 12, 2008, killing tens of thousands of people.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跷 describes raising the foot or standing on tiptoe, as with stilts.
尧 (yáo) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 跷's qiāo — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他踩着高跷在街上表演。
example.pinyin: Tā cǎi zhe gāoqiāo zài jiē shàng biǎoyǎn.
example.english: He performed in the street walking on stilts.
example.fact: 高跷 (gāoqiāo), stilt-walking, is a traditional folk performance art in northern China, often part of Lunar New Year parades alongside dragon and lion dances.

components.note: 玨 (a form of 王/玉, jade) doesn't mean jade literally here — it's shared with 琶 to write the two-syllable instrument name 琵琶 as a matching pair.
比 (bǐ) shares 琵's vowel and a related initial consonant, though the tone differs — a fairly close, if not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 她从小学习弹琵琶。
example.pinyin: Tā cóngxiǎo xuéxí tán pípá.
example.english: She has studied playing the pípá since childhood.
example.fact: 琵 and 琶 almost never appear apart from each other — like a handful of other Chinese words, the two characters exist only as a fixed pair naming one thing, the pípá lute.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 憨 describes a simple, naive, or foolishly honest disposition.
敢 (gǎn) shares 憨's final -an, though the initial consonant and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 他一脸憨笑,看起来很老实。
example.pinyin: Tā yì liǎn hānxiào, kàn qǐlái hěn lǎoshi.
example.english: He wore a naive, good-natured smile and looked very honest.
example.fact: 憨 usually carries a warm, affectionate undertone in Chinese rather than a purely negative one — 憨厚 (hānhòu) describes someone endearingly simple and good-natured, closer to 'guileless' than 'stupid.'

components.note: 虫 (a small creature) — 蜗 names snails.
呙 (guō) shares 蜗's rhyme and tone, though the initial consonant differs — a fairly close, if not exact, match.

example.hanzi: 蜗牛在叶子上慢慢爬行。
example.pinyin: Wōniú zài yèzi shàng mànmàn páxíng.
example.english: The snail crawls slowly across the leaf.
example.fact: 蜗居 (wōjū), literally 'to live like a snail,' is a common modern Chinese term for cramped, tiny housing — comparing a small apartment to a snail's shell.

components.note: 虫 (a small creature) — 螅 names small aquatic invertebrates.
息 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 螅's reading.

example.hanzi: 水螅是一种生活在水中的小动物。
example.pinyin: Shuǐxī shì yì zhǒng shēnghuó zài shuǐ zhōng de xiǎo dòngwù.
example.english: The hydra is a small animal that lives in water.
example.fact: 水螅 (Hydra) is famous among biologists for its extraordinary regenerative ability — it can regrow its entire body from just a small fragment, and some researchers consider it biologically almost non-aging.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 惴 describes a state of anxious apprehension.
耑 (duān) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 惴's zhuì — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他惴惴不安地等待考试结果。
example.pinyin: Tā zhuìzhuì-bù'ān de děngdài kǎoshì jiéguǒ.
example.english: He waited anxiously and uneasily for the exam results.
example.fact: 惴惴不安 (zhuìzhuì-bù'ān), 'anxious and uneasy,' is a common four-character phrase for nervous anticipation — it appears as early as the ancient poetry collection Shijing (Book of Songs).

etymologyHint: An axe 戈 with blades on both sides 龺

components.note: 戟 depicts a composite weapon that combines a straight thrusting blade with a hooked axe-blade 戈 mounted to one side — the halberd's signature two-in-one design.

example.hanzi: 戟是古代常见的一种兵器。
example.pinyin: Jǐ shì gǔdài chángjiàn de yì zhǒng bīngqì.
example.english: The halberd was a common weapon in ancient times.
example.fact: The 戟 combined a spear's thrusting point with an axe-like side blade, letting a soldier stab, hook, or slash with a single weapon — a design found in many ancient cultures' polearms, not just China's.

components.note: 匚 (a box, a container) — 匮 originally described a container being empty or exhausted.
贵 (guì) shares 匮's final and tone, and a closely related initial consonant — a fairly close match.

example.hanzi: 山区的水资源十分匮乏。
example.pinyin: Shānqū de shuǐ zīyuán shífēn kuìfá.
example.english: Water resources in the mountain region are extremely scarce.
example.fact: 匮乏 (kuìfá), 'scarce, in short supply,' is standard vocabulary in Chinese for describing shortages of resources, from water and food to funding and talent.

components.note: 心 (heart, but used generally for the body's condition) — 恙 names illness or indisposition.
羊 (yáng) gives a sound close to 恙's reading yàng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他身体安然无恙。
example.pinyin: Tā shēntǐ ānrán wúyàng.
example.english: He is safe and sound, without any ailment.
example.fact: 安然无恙 (ānrán-wúyàng), 'safe and sound,' is the standard Chinese phrase for confirming someone has come through a dangerous situation unharmed — 恙 itself almost never appears outside this and a few similar set phrases.

meanings: to smooth hair with a wet brush
(of a mouth, wing etc) to close lightly

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抿 describes lightly pressing or smoothing something with the hand or lips, as in pressing the lips together.
民 (mín) gives a sound close to 抿's reading mǐn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她抿了一口茶,没有说话。
example.pinyin: Tā mǐn le yì kǒu chá, méiyǒu shuōhuà.
example.english: She took a small, closed-lip sip of tea without saying anything.
example.fact: 抿 describes a very specific small action — pressing the lips together, whether to smooth lipstick, suppress a smile, or take the smallest possible sip of a drink.

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — 桢 named a hardwood tree used for building supports and posts.
贞 (zhēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 桢's reading.

example.hanzi: 他给孩子取名叫桢。
example.pinyin: Tā gěi háizi qǐmíng jiào Zhēn.
example.english: He named his child Zhen.
example.fact: 桢 has become mainly a name character in modern Chinese — its original meaning, a supporting post or hardwood beam, survives today chiefly in given names, where it suggests steadfast strength.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — early writing paper and note-slips were made from bamboo or bamboo-derived material.
戋 (jiān) gives the sound — an exact match with 笺's reading.

example.hanzi: 她在信笺上写下了自己的心事。
example.pinyin: Tā zài xìnjiān shàng xiěxià le zìjǐ de xīnshì.
example.english: She wrote down her private thoughts on stationery paper.
example.fact: 笺 named decorative stationery paper, often printed with faint patterns — 花笺 (huājiān), 'flower-patterned notepaper,' was especially prized by literati for writing poetry and letters in imperial China.

components.note: 虫 (a small creature) — 蛤 names clams and other shellfish.
合 (hé) shares 蛤's initial consonant and tone, though the vowel differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 池塘里传来阵阵蛤蟆的叫声。
example.pinyin: Chítáng lǐ chuánlái zhèn zhèn háma de jiào shēng.
example.english: Croaking sounds come again and again from the pond's toads.
example.fact: This character has two unrelated readings depending on the word: há in 蛤蟆 (háma, 'toad, frog') and gé in 蛤蜊 (gélí, 'clam') — one character covering both an amphibian and a shellfish.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 瞳 names the pupil of the eye.
童 (tóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 瞳's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的瞳孔在黑暗中逐渐放大。
example.pinyin: Tā de tóngkǒng zài hēi'àn zhōng zhújiàn fàngdà.
example.english: His pupils gradually dilated in the darkness.
example.fact: 瞳孔 (tóngkǒng), 'pupil,' dilates and contracts to control how much light enters the eye — a reflex so fast and involuntary that it's used as a hard-to-fake indicator of alertness.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — most early medicines were derived from herbs and plants, hence 藥's plant radical.

樂 is tagged as the phonetic element here (an old graphic root shared with 'music/joy'), but it bears no resemblance to yào in modern pronunciation — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 良藥苦口,卻對身體有益。
example.pinyin: Liángyào kǔkǒu, què duì shēntǐ yǒuyì.
example.english: Good medicine tastes bitter, yet is good for the body.
example.fact: 藥 is the traditional form of the simplified character 药 ('medicine'); it remains the standard spelling in Taiwan and Hong Kong today.

components.note: 瓜 (gourd, melon) — a 瓢 is a dipper traditionally made from a dried, hollowed-out gourd.
票 (piào) gives a sound close to 瓢's reading piáo, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他用瓢舀水喝。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng piáo yǎo shuǐ hē.
example.english: He scooped water with a gourd dipper to drink.
example.fact: 瓢 dippers made from dried bottle gourds were a common household tool across rural China for centuries before being widely replaced by metal and plastic ladles.

meanings: robe of a Buddhist monk or nun

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 衹 was originally a robe-related character before being borrowed as a variant of 只 (zhǐ, 'only, merely').
氏 (shì) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 衹's zhǐ — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他衹是随便说说而已。
example.pinyin: Tā zhǐ shì suíbiàn shuōshuo éryǐ.
example.english: He was just saying it casually, nothing more.
example.fact: 衹 is a rare variant of the everyday word 只 (zhǐ, 'only'); modern Chinese almost always uses the simpler 只 instead, leaving 衹 mostly to appear in older or more formal printed texts.

etymologyHint: A balance 平 used to measure grain 禾

components.note: 禾 (grain) — the 秤 (steelyard balance) was originally used mainly for weighing grain.
平 (level, balanced) — a working scale must sit level and balanced; 平's own reading píng isn't close to chèng, so the pairing works through meaning rather than sound.

example.hanzi: 商人用秤称量货物的重量。
example.pinyin: Shāngrén yòng chèng chēngliáng huòwù de zhòngliàng.
example.english: The merchant uses a scale to weigh the goods.
example.fact: The traditional Chinese steelyard balance (秤), a rod-and-sliding-weight design, works on the same lever principle as ancient Roman and Egyptian balance scales — a solution independently arrived at by multiple civilizations.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跺 describes stamping one's foot.
朵 (duǒ) gives a sound close to 跺's reading duò, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她气得直跺脚。
example.pinyin: Tā qì de zhí duòjiǎo.
example.english: She was so angry that she kept stamping her feet.
example.fact: 跺脚 (duòjiǎo), 'to stamp one's feet,' is a common physical expression of frustration or impatience in Chinese, much as in English, and appears frequently in descriptions of characters losing their temper.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 潦 describes flooding, puddles, or heavy rain.
尞 is the phonetic root behind a family of liáo-reading characters like 缭 and 燎, but 潦's own reading here, lǎo, has drifted away from that family — an exception within the group.

example.hanzi: 潦水尽而寒潭清,这是《滕王阁序》中的名句。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshuǐ jìn ér hántán qīng, zhè shì Téngwánggé Xù zhōng de míngjù.
example.english: 'As the floodwaters recede, the cold pool turns clear' — this is a famous line from the Preface to the Prince Teng Pavilion.
example.fact: 潦水 (lǎoshuǐ), 'rainwater, floodwater,' appears in this well-known line from Wang Bo's Tang-dynasty prose-poem 滕王阁序, one of the most celebrated pieces of classical Chinese prose.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 芹 names celery.
斤 (jīn) shares 芹's final -in and a closely related initial consonant, though the tone differs — a fairly close match.

example.hanzi: 妈妈买了一些新鲜的芹菜。
example.pinyin: Māma mǎi le yìxiē xīnxiān de qíncài.
example.english: Mom bought some fresh celery.
example.fact: 芹菜 (qíncài), Chinese celery, has thinner stalks and a stronger flavor than the celery common in Western supermarkets, and it's typically stir-fried rather than eaten raw.

meanings: a sound made to get a horse to move forward

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哒 is a modern onomatopoeic character for a clicking or clopping sound, like a horse's hooves.
达 (dá) gives a sound close to 哒's reading dā, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 马蹄哒哒地敲在石板路上。
example.pinyin: Mǎtí dādā de qiāo zài shíbǎn lù shàng.
example.english: The horse's hooves clip-clopped on the stone-paved road.
example.fact: 哒 is a relatively modern character, created mainly to write onomatopoeia and internet-slang expressions like 好的哒 (hǎodedā), a cutesy way of saying 'okay' popular in casual online Chinese.

components.note: 力 (strength, effort) — 饬 describes putting things in order or issuing a directive that requires effort to carry out.
饣 is tagged as the phonetic element here (from 食, historically shí), but it bears no real resemblance to 饬's reading chì — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 上级饬令各部门加强安全检查。
example.pinyin: Shàngjí chìlìng gè bùmén jiāqiáng ānquán jiǎnchá.
example.english: The higher authority ordered all departments to strengthen safety inspections.
example.fact: 饬 is a formal, bureaucratic character today, appearing mainly in official documents and set phrases like 饬令 (chìlìng, 'to order, to direct') — a register far more formal than everyday commands.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 栩 originally named a species of oak.
羽 (yǔ) shares 栩's final and tone, though the initial consonant differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 他讲得栩栩如生。
example.pinyin: Tā jiǎng de xǔxǔ-rúshēng.
example.english: He told it so vividly it seemed lifelike.
example.fact: 栩栩如生 (xǔxǔ-rúshēng), 'vivid and lifelike,' is a common idiom for praising realistic art, writing, or performances — 栩 itself almost never appears outside this one phrase.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 曦 describes the light of the rising or morning sun.
羲 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 曦's reading.

example.hanzi: 晨曦透过窗帘照进房间。
example.pinyin: Chénxī tòuguò chuānglián zhào jìn fángjiān.
example.english: The morning sunlight streams through the curtains into the room.
example.fact: 晨曦 (chénxī), 'morning sunlight, dawn light,' is a favorite poetic word in Chinese for the soft light just after sunrise, distinct from the plainer, more neutral word 阳光 (sunlight in general).

meanings: used in 骷髏|骷髅[ku1 lou2]

components.note: 骨 (bone) — 骷 names a skull or skeleton.
古 (gǔ) shares 骷's vowel and a related initial consonant, though the tone differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 海盗旗上画着骷髅图案。
example.pinyin: Hǎidào qí shàng huà zhe kūlóu tú'àn.
example.english: The pirate flag is painted with a skull design.
example.fact: 骷髅 (kūlóu), 'skull, skeleton,' is the word behind the Jolly Roger's Chinese nickname 骷髅旗 (kūlóu qí), 'skull-and-crossbones flag.'

components.note: 女 (woman) — 嫡 originally distinguished the principal wife and her children from those of secondary wives or concubines.
啇 gives the sound, matching 嫡's reading dí, and is the same phonetic root shared by 敌 (dí, 'enemy') and 滴 (dī, 'a drop').

example.hanzi: 在古代,嫡子通常享有继承权。
example.pinyin: Zài gǔdài, dízǐ tōngcháng xiǎngyǒu jìchéngquán.
example.english: In ancient times, the son of the principal wife usually held inheritance rights.
