example.fact: 嫡 marks a once-crucial legal distinction in imperial China between 嫡 (children of the principal wife) and 庶 (children of concubines) — a difference that could decide who inherited a family's title, property, or throne.

meanings: to stew in soy sauce and spices
etymologyHint: A container used to brine pickles

components.note: The traditional form 鹵 is thought to picture grains of salt scattered inside a container or sack — an image tied to 卤's original meaning of natural brine or alkaline salt.

example.hanzi: 这只鸡是卤鸡,味道很香。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī jī shì lǔjī, wèidào hěn xiāng.
example.english: This chicken is braised in soy-spiced brine; it smells delicious.
example.fact: 卤 (lǔ), 'to stew in a soy-and-spice brine,' names one of the most common Chinese home-cooking techniques — 卤味 (lǔwèi), brine-stewed foods like eggs, tofu, and meat, are a fixture of Chinese street food and takeout.

example.hanzi: 曹丕是曹操的儿子。
example.pinyin: Cáo Pī shì Cáo Cāo de érzi.
example.english: Cao Pi was Cao Cao's son.
example.fact: 曹丕, whose name uses this character meaning 'great, grand,' ended the Han dynasty in 220 CE by founding the state of Wei, becoming one of the central figures of the Three Kingdoms period.

components.note: 髟 (long hair) — 鬓 names the hair at the temples.
宾 (bīn) gives a sound close to 鬓's reading bìn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他的两鬓已经斑白了。
example.pinyin: Tā de liǎng bìn yǐjīng bānbái le.
example.english: The hair at both his temples has already turned gray.
example.fact: 两鬓斑白 (liǎng bìn bānbái), 'graying at both temples,' is a common literary way in Chinese to indicate someone has grown older, often used with a tone of either dignity or wistfulness.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 梓 names the catalpa tree, prized for printing blocks and fine woodworking.
辛 (xīn) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 梓's zǐ — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 这本书采用了传统的梓木刻版印刷。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū cǎiyòng le chuántǒng de zǐmù kèbǎn yìnshuā.
example.english: This book was printed using traditional catalpa-wood woodblock printing.
example.fact: 付梓 (fùzǐ), literally 'to hand over to catalpa wood,' is a classical Chinese expression meaning 'to send to print, to publish' — from the once-common practice of carving printing blocks from catalpa wood.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗖 is an onomatopoeia for a whooshing or whizzing sound.
叟 (sǒu) gives a sound close to 嗖's reading sōu, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 子弹嗖的一声飞了过去。
example.pinyin: Zǐdàn sōu de yì shēng fēi le guòqù.
example.english: The bullet whizzed past with a 'sōu' sound.
example.fact: 嗖 is a pure sound-word describing something moving very fast through the air — bullets, arrows, and swift punches are all commonly described with 嗖 in Chinese action writing.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 惦 describes keeping someone or something in mind.
店 (diàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 惦's reading.

example.hanzi: 妈妈总是惦记着在外的孩子。
example.pinyin: Māma zǒngshì diànjì zhe zài wài de háizi.
example.english: Mom always keeps thinking of her children who are away from home.
example.fact: 惦记 (diànjì), 'to think of, to worry about someone with care,' describes a gentle, ongoing concern — commonly used for the way parents think about children who have moved away.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浚 describes dredging a river or waterway to deepen it.
夋 gives the sound — an exact match with 浚's reading jùn, the same phonetic root shared by 竣.

example.hanzi: 政府决定疏浚这条河道。
example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ juédìng shūjùn zhè tiáo hédào.
example.english: The government decided to dredge this waterway.
example.fact: 疏浚 (shūjùn), 'to dredge,' is the standard engineering term in Chinese for clearing silt and debris from rivers, canals, and harbors to keep them navigable.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咔 is a modern onomatopoeic character for a sharp clicking or snapping sound.
卡 (kǎ) gives a sound close to 咔's reading kā, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 相机咔的一声拍下了照片。
example.pinyin: Xiàngjī kā de yì shēng pāixià le zhàopiàn.
example.english: The camera clicked and took the photo.
example.fact: 咔 is a modern character built specifically to write the click of a camera shutter or a snapping sound, part of a wave of new onomatopoeic characters coined as Chinese absorbed more foreign technology and media.

components.note: 艹 (grass, small plants) — used here for its association with something small or insignificant.

貌 (appearance, looks) — regarding someone's appearance as beneath notice gave 藐 its sense of 'to belittle, to disregard'; 貌's own reading mào isn't close to miǎo, so this is a meaning link rather than a sound one.

example.hanzi: 他从不藐视比自己弱小的人。
example.pinyin: Tā cóngbù miǎoshì bǐ zìjǐ ruòxiǎo de rén.
example.english: He never looks down on those weaker than himself.
example.fact: 藐视 (miǎoshì), 'to look down on, to despise,' shares its second character with 视 (to look, to view) — many Chinese words for scorn are literally built from 'looking' verbs plus a modifier, like 轻视 and 蔑视.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 荃 named a fragrant herb, later mainly kept as a name character.
全 (quán) gives the sound — an exact match with 荃's reading.

example.hanzi: 荃是古代典籍中提到的一种香草。
example.pinyin: Quán shì gǔdài diǎnjí zhōng tídào de yì zhǒng xiāngcǎo.
example.english: Quán is a fragrant herb mentioned in ancient texts.
example.fact: 荃 appears in the Chuci (楚辞), an ancient anthology of poetry associated with Qu Yuan, where fragrant plants like 荃 are often used as symbols for a virtuous ruler or a noble character.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 唧 is an onomatopoeia for chirping or squeaking sounds.
即 (jí) gives a sound close to 唧's reading jī, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 夏夜里,虫子唧唧地叫着。
example.pinyin: Xiàyè lǐ, chóngzi jījī de jiào zhe.
example.english: On summer nights, insects chirp incessantly.
example.fact: 唧唧 (jījī) is the classic Chinese onomatopoeia for insect chirping — it opens the famous folk ballad 木兰诗 (Ballad of Mulan): '唧唧复唧唧,木兰当户织' ('chirp, chirp, and chirp again, Mulan weaves at the door').

components.note: 玉 (jade) — an imperial 玺 seal was carved from jade or other precious material.
尔 (ěr) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 玺's xǐ — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 皇帝的玉玺是权力的象征。
example.pinyin: Huángdì de yùxǐ shì quánlì de xiàngzhēng.
example.english: The emperor's jade seal was a symbol of power.
example.fact: The Chinese imperial seal (玉玺) was considered so central to legitimate rule that possessing the genuine historical seal was treated by some as proof of a ruler's authority — its loss during periods of chaos was recorded as a major crisis.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汛 names a seasonal rise in water level, a flood tide.
卂 (xùn) gives the sound — an exact match with 汛's reading.

example.hanzi: 每年夏天都会有防汛的任务。
example.pinyin: Měinián xiàtiān dōu huì yǒu fángxùn de rènwù.
example.english: Every summer there are flood-prevention tasks to carry out.
example.fact: 防汛 (fángxùn), 'flood prevention and control,' is a major seasonal effort in China each summer, when rivers like the Yangtze and Yellow River face their highest risk of overflowing from monsoon rains.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铐 names metal shackles or handcuffs.
考 (kǎo) gives a sound close to 铐's reading kào, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 警察给犯人戴上了手铐。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá gěi fànrén dài shàng le shǒukào.
example.english: The police put handcuffs on the criminal.
example.fact: 手铐 (shǒukào), 'handcuffs,' is a relatively recent compound word in Chinese — 铐 itself only came to name this specific restraint device as Western-style policing equipment became common in the 20th century.

meanings: used in 髑髏|髑髅[du2 lou2] and 骷髏|骷髅[ku1 lou2]

components.note: 骨 (bone) — 髅 names a skull, paired with 骷 in 骷髅.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 髅's reading.

example.hanzi: 骷髅头图案常出现在警示标志上。
example.pinyin: Kūlóutóu tú'àn cháng chūxiàn zài jǐngshì biāozhì shàng.
example.english: Skull-and-crossbones designs often appear on warning signs.
example.fact: 骷髅, the word 髅 almost always appears in, is the standard Chinese term for both a real skeleton and the stylized skull-and-crossbones symbol used to mark danger, from pirate flags to poison labels.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渤 names the Bohai Sea.
勃 (bó) gives the sound — an exact match with 渤's reading.

example.hanzi: 渤海是中国的内海。
example.pinyin: Bóhǎi shì Zhōngguó de nèihǎi.
example.english: The Bohai Sea is an inland sea of China.
example.fact: 渤海 (Bohai Sea) is nearly enclosed by the Liaodong and Shandong peninsulas, making it one of China's most sheltered seas and one of the shallowest major seas in the world, with an average depth under 20 meters.

components.note: 皿 is a picture of a shallow dish or vessel seen from the side, with a wide mouth and a base — it's also the radical found in characters for bowls, plates, and basins like 盘, 盆, and 盖.

example.hanzi: 厨房里摆着各种碗碟器皿。
example.pinyin: Chúfáng lǐ bǎi zhe gèzhǒng wǎndié qìmǐn.
example.english: All sorts of bowls and plates are arranged in the kitchen.
example.fact: 皿 rarely stands alone in modern Chinese; it survives mainly as a radical inside other characters for containers and dishes, and in the general term 器皿 (qìmǐn), 'vessels, containers.'

etymologyHint: Bamboo ⺮ bindings 㧜; 㧜 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — a 箍 hoop was traditionally made by binding strips of bamboo or metal around something.
㧜 is a rare component whose own reading isn't well established in modern reference, so its link to 箍's sound is best treated as historical rather than a clear match.

example.hanzi: 木桶外面用铁箍加固。
example.pinyin: Mùtǒng wàimiàn yòng tiě gū jiāgù.
example.english: The wooden bucket is reinforced on the outside with an iron hoop.
example.fact: 箍 names the tight-fitting magic headband (紧箍儿) that binds the Monkey King Sun Wukong's powers in the classic novel Journey to the West, controlled by a spell called 紧箍咒.

etymologyHint: Food 饣 stuffed in a hole 臽; 臽 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 饣 (food) — 馅 names the filling or stuffing inside food like dumplings.
臽 shares 馅's exact reading xiàn — the same phonetic root also appears in 陷 (xiàn, 'to sink into, a trap'), evoking something tucked or sunk inside.

example.hanzi: 这个包子的馅是猪肉和白菜。
example.pinyin: Zhège bāozi de xiàn shì zhūròu hé báicài.
example.english: This steamed bun's filling is pork and cabbage.
example.fact: 馅 also appears in the figurative expression 露馅 (lòuxiàn), literally 'to expose the filling,' meaning to accidentally reveal a secret or expose a lie — much like the English phrase 'to spill the beans.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汾 names the Fen River in Shanxi.
分 (fēn) gives a sound close to 汾's reading fén, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 汾河是山西省最大的河流。
example.pinyin: Fén Hé shì Shānxī Shěng zuìdà de héliú.
example.english: The Fen River is Shanxi province's largest river.
example.fact: The Fen River valley gives its name to Fenjiu (汾酒), one of China's most historic distilled liquors, with a documented history stretching back well over a thousand years.

etymologyHint: Arms 戈 surrounding the country 丶

components.note: 戍 depicts a weapon 戈 with a person represented by the small stroke beside it — the image of someone standing guard with a weapon, giving 戍 its meaning 'to garrison, to guard the frontier.'

example.hanzi: 士兵常年戍守边疆。
example.pinyin: Shìbīng chángnián shùshǒu biānjiāng.
example.english: Soldiers guard the frontier all year round.
example.fact: 戍 gives its name to 戍卒 (shùzú), the border-garrison conscripts of ancient China — the peasant uprising that helped topple the Qin dynasty in 209 BCE was led by Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, two such conscripted 戍卒.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痔 names hemorrhoids, an ailment.
寺 (sì) shares 痔's vowel and tone, though the initial consonant differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 久坐容易引发痔疮。
example.pinyin: Jiǔ zuò róngyì yǐnfā zhìchuāng.
example.english: Sitting for long periods can easily bring on hemorrhoids.
example.fact: 痔 almost always appears in the compound 痔疮 (zhìchuāng), and doctors commonly cite prolonged sitting and low-fiber diets as two of the most preventable risk factors for the condition.

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 褶 names a pleat or fold in fabric.
習 (xí) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 褶's zhě — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 她把裙子上的褶熨平了。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ qúnzi shàng de zhě yùn píng le.
example.english: She ironed the pleats in her skirt flat.
example.fact: 褶皱 (zhězhòu), 'wrinkles, folds,' describes fabric creases but is also standard geology vocabulary in Chinese for the folded rock layers formed when tectonic plates compress the earth's crust.

components.note: 耳 (ear) — 聆 describes listening attentively.
令 (lìng) gives a sound close to 聆's reading líng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 大家安静地聆听老师的讲解。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā ānjìng de língtīng lǎoshī de jiǎngjiě.
example.english: Everyone listened quietly and attentively to the teacher's explanation.
example.fact: 聆听 (língtīng) implies a more respectful, attentive kind of listening than the plain verb 听 — it's often used for listening to teachers, elders, speeches, or music with focused attention.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 涎 names saliva.
延 (yán) shares 涎's final -ian and tone, though the initial consonant differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 小狗看到食物就开始流涎。
example.pinyin: Xiǎogǒu kàndào shíwù jiù kāishǐ liú xián.
example.english: As soon as the puppy sees food, it starts drooling.
example.fact: 垂涎 (chuíxián), literally 'to let saliva hang down,' is the classical root of the modern idiom 垂涎三尺 (chuíxián-sānchǐ), 'drooling three feet,' a hyperbolic way of describing intense desire or envy.

components.note: 水 (water) — mercury is a liquid metal, hence the water radical, even though placed unusually at the bottom of the character.
工 (gōng) gives a sound close to 汞's reading gǒng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 水银的化学名称是汞。
example.pinyin: Shuǐyín de huàxué míngchēng shì gǒng.
example.english: The chemical name for quicksilver is mercury (gǒng).
example.fact: Mercury is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature (the other being bromine) — its Chinese name, 水银 ('silver water'), and English name 'quicksilver' both describe its shimmering, liquid-metal appearance.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渍 describes soaking something in liquid, or a stain left behind.
责 (zé) shares 渍's initial consonant, though the vowel and tone differ — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 衣服上有一块油渍洗不掉。
example.pinyin: Yīfu shàng yǒu yí kuài yóuzì xǐ bú diào.
example.english: There's an oil stain on the clothes that won't wash out.
example.fact: 渍 covers both the process (to soak, as in 腌渍 yānzì, 'to pickle') and the result (a stain, as in 油渍 yóuzì, 'oil stain') — one character for both soaking something and the mark it leaves behind.

example.hanzi: 这座建筑修得美轮美奂。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò jiànzhù xiū de měilún-měihuàn.
example.english: This building was built to be magnificently beautiful.
example.fact: 奂 survives in modern Mandarin almost entirely through the idiom 美轮美奂 (měilún-měihuàn), 'magnificent and splendid,' typically used to praise the physical beauty of a newly built or newly renovated structure.

etymologyHint: The top 颠 of a mountain 山; 颠 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 巅 names the very top, the summit, of a mountain.
颠 (the top of the head, or to topple) shares 巅's exact reading diān, and its 'topmost' sense reinforces the idea of a summit.

example.hanzi: 他们终于登上了山巅。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zhōngyú dēngshàng le shāndiān.
example.english: They finally climbed to the mountain's summit.
example.fact: 巅峰 (diānfēng), literally 'summit and peak,' is commonly used figuratively in Chinese for the height of a career, an era, or an achievement — much like the English word 'pinnacle.'

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 疣 names a wart, a skin growth.
尤 (yóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 疣's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的手上长了一个疣。
example.pinyin: Tā de shǒu shàng zhǎng le yí gè yóu.
example.english: A wart grew on his hand.
example.fact: Most common warts (疣) are caused by strains of human papillomavirus (HPV) infecting the skin's outer layer — the wart-causing strains themselves are generally harmless, distinct from the strains linked to more serious conditions.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 傩 describes a person performing an exorcism ritual, a masked dance meant to drive away evil spirits.
难 (nán) shares 傩's initial consonant and tone, though the vowel differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 傩戏是一种古老的民间戏剧形式。
example.pinyin: Nuóxì shì yì zhǒng gǔlǎo de mínjiān xìjù xíngshì.
example.english: Nuo opera is an ancient form of folk theater.
example.fact: 傩戏 (nuóxì), a masked ritual drama meant to exorcise evil spirits and disease, has been performed in parts of rural China for well over a thousand years and is recognized as an important form of intangible cultural heritage.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, a road) — 逵 names a major crossroads or thoroughfare.
坴 (lù) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 逵's kuí — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他的名字里有一个逵字。
example.pinyin: Tā de míngzi lǐ yǒu yí gè kuí zì.
example.english: His name contains the character kuí.
example.fact: 逵 is a fairly rare character today, surviving mainly in given names and classical place names for major crossroads — its everyday meaning has been almost entirely replaced by 大道 or simply 路.

components.note: 老 (old) — 耆 describes an elderly person, especially one aged sixty or seventy.
日 (rì) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 耆's qí — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 他是村里的耆老,很受尊敬。
example.pinyin: Tā shì cūn lǐ de qílǎo, hěn shòu zūnjìng.
example.english: He is a village elder, and is very much respected.
example.fact: 耆老 (qílǎo), 'a respected elder,' reflects an old Chinese social ranking of old age by decade — some classical texts specifically labeled a person in their sixties as 耆 and in their seventies as 老, distinguishing finer gradations of old age than English typically does.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蟋 names crickets, paired with 蟀 in 蟋蟀.
悉 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 蟋's reading.

example.hanzi: 秋天的夜里能听到蟋蟀的叫声。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān de yè lǐ néng tīngdào xīshuài de jiào shēng.
example.english: On autumn nights you can hear crickets chirping.
example.fact: Cricket fighting (斗蟋蟀) has been a popular pastime in China for centuries — prized fighting crickets have historically been bought and sold for significant sums, with dedicated breeders and trainers.

components.note: 鱼 (fish, broadened to aquatic creatures) — 鳄 names crocodiles and alligators.
咢 (è) gives the sound — an exact match with 鳄's reading.

example.hanzi: 扬子鳄是中国特有的一种鳄鱼。
example.pinyin: Yángzǐ È shì Zhōngguó tèyǒu de yì zhǒng èyú.
example.english: The Chinese alligator is a species of crocodilian unique to China.
example.fact: The Chinese alligator (扬子鳄) is critically endangered in the wild, with only a small remaining wild population in the lower Yangtze region, though thousands survive in captive breeding programs.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 讹 describes false or misleading speech, an error or a swindle.
化 (huà) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 讹's é — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 这个消息在传播中被讹传了。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi zài chuánbò zhōng bèi échuán le.
example.english: This piece of news got garbled and distorted as it spread.
example.fact: 讹传 (échuán), 'a garbled rumor, a distorted report,' describes information that mutates as it passes from person to person — the same phenomenon studied in psychology under names like the 'telephone game' effect.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 膺 originally named the chest.
䧹 (yīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 膺's reading.

example.hanzi: 他义愤填膺,难以平静。
example.pinyin: Tā yìfèn-tiányīng, nányǐ píngjìng.
example.english: He was filled with righteous indignation, unable to calm down.
example.fact: 义愤填膺 (yìfèn-tiányīng), 'righteous indignation filling the chest,' is a common four-character idiom for being overcome with moral outrage at some injustice.

meanings: (coll.) to gush out; to spurt out

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹿 describes leaping or bounding suddenly upward or forward.
窜 (cuàn) gives a sound close to 蹿's reading cuān, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 猴子一下子蹿到了树上。
example.pinyin: Hóuzi yíxiàzi cuān dào le shù shàng.
example.english: The monkey leapt up into the tree in an instant.
example.fact: 蹿 describes a quick, explosive upward or forward motion — it's often used for flames 'leaping' higher, prices 'shooting' up, or a person's height suddenly 'shooting up' during a growth spurt.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — a 筏 raft was traditionally built by lashing together bamboo poles or logs.
伐 (fá) gives the sound — an exact match with 筏's reading.

example.hanzi: 他们乘着竹筏顺流而下。
example.pinyin: Tāmen chéng zhe zhúfá shùnliú ér xià.
example.english: They floated downstream on a bamboo raft.
example.fact: 竹筏 (zhúfá), bamboo rafts, remain a common way to move tourists and goods along scenic rivers in parts of southern China, such as the Li River near Guilin.

components.note: 金 (metal) — a 釜 was an ancient cauldron or cooking pot, usually made of bronze or iron.
父 (fù) gives a sound close to 釜's reading fǔ, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 破釜沉舟,他决心不再后退。
example.pinyin: Pòfǔ-chénzhōu, tā juéxīn bú zài hòutuì.
example.english: Breaking the cauldrons and sinking the boats, he resolved never to retreat.
example.fact: 破釜沉舟 (pòfǔ-chénzhōu), 'to smash the cauldrons and sink the boats,' comes from a real historical episode: the general Xiang Yu destroyed his own army's cooking pots and boats before a decisive battle, forcing his soldiers to fight with no hope of retreat.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沂 names the Yi River in Shandong.
斤 (jīn) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 沂's yí — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 沂蒙山区是著名的革命老区。
example.pinyin: Yíméng Shānqū shì zhùmíng de gémìng lǎoqū.
example.english: The Yimeng mountain area is a well-known former revolutionary base region.
example.fact: 沂 names the Yi River, whose valley combines with the nearby Meng mountains to form 沂蒙 (Yimeng), a region known in modern Chinese history as a key Communist base area during the war against Japan and the civil war.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 坯 names unfired clay or mud brick, before it's baked or dried.
丕 (pī) gives the sound — an exact match with 坯's reading.

example.hanzi: 陶匠先把陶土做成坯,再放入窑中烧制。
example.pinyin: Táojiàng xiān bǎ táotǔ zuò chéng pī, zài fàngrù yáo zhōng shāozhì.
example.english: The potter first shapes the clay into an unfired form, then fires it in a kiln.
example.fact: 坯 names the crucial in-between stage of pottery-making — the shaped but not-yet-fired clay object — a concept important enough in Chinese ceramics to have its own dedicated character.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峦 names a mountain range, or a series of peaks.

䜌 gives the sound — an exact match with 峦's reading luán, and is also the root behind 孪 (luán, 'twin'); the same root has drifted into very different-sounding characters like 蛮 (mán) and 湾 (wān) over time.

example.hanzi: 远处的山峦连绵不绝。
example.pinyin: Yuǎnchù de shānluán liánmián bùjué.
example.english: The distant mountain ranges stretch on without end.
example.fact: 山峦 (shānluán), 'mountain ranges,' is a favorite word in Chinese landscape poetry and painting descriptions for rolling, overlapping peaks stretching into the distance.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 茬 originally named crop stubble left in a field after harvest.
在 (zài) is the phonetic element tagged here, but its modern reading bears little resemblance to 茬's chá — the connection today is historical rather than audible.

example.hanzi: 收割后,地里留下了一片麦茬。
example.pinyin: Shōugē hòu, dìlǐ liúxià le yí piàn màichá.
example.english: After the harvest, a stretch of wheat stubble was left in the field.
example.fact: 茬 has picked up a lively modern slang sense in the phrase 找茬 (zhǎochá), literally 'to look for stubble' — meaning to nitpick or deliberately find fault with someone.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摒 describes pushing something aside or casting it off.
屏 (píng) shares 摒's final -ing and a closely related initial consonant, though the tone differs — a fairly close match.

example.hanzi: 他摒弃了旧的偏见。
example.pinyin: Tā bìngqì le jiù de piānjiàn.
example.english: He cast aside his old prejudices.
example.fact: 摒弃 (bìngqì), 'to discard, to cast aside,' is often used for abandoning outdated ideas, bad habits, or old grudges — an act of deliberate, decisive rejection rather than simple forgetting.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蟀 names crickets, paired with 蟋 in 蟋蟀.
率, in its shuài reading, gives the sound — an exact match with 蟀's reading.

example.hanzi: 蟋蟀在草丛里鸣叫。
example.pinyin: Xīshuài zài cǎocóng lǐ míngjiào.
example.english: Crickets chirp among the grass.
example.fact: 蟀 never appears alone in modern Chinese — like 蝙 and 蝠 (bat) or 琵 and 琶 (lute), it exists only as half of the fixed two-character word 蟋蟀, 'cricket.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撵 describes driving someone away, chasing them off by force.
辇 (niǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 撵's reading.

example.hanzi: 他被老板撵出了办公室。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi lǎobǎn niǎn chū le bàngōngshì.
example.english: He was chased out of the office by his boss.
example.fact: 撵 is a distinctly colloquial, spoken-register word for 'to drive away, to chase off' — more formal writing generally prefers 驱逐 (qūzhú) or 赶走 (gǎnzǒu) for the same idea.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浒 names the bank or shore of a body of water.
许 (xǔ) shares 浒's final and tone, though the initial consonant differs — a partial rather than close match.

example.hanzi: 《水浒传》是中国四大名著之一。
example.pinyin: 《Shuǐhǔ Zhuàn》 shì Zhōngguó sìdà míngzhù zhī yī.
example.english: Water Margin is one of the Four Great Classical Novels of China.
example.fact: 浒 is known almost entirely through its role in 水浒传 (Shuǐhǔ Zhuàn, 'Water Margin'), a 14th-century novel about a band of outlaws — one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature.

meanings: used in 繽紛|缤纷[bin1 fen1]

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 缤 describes something richly varied and abundant, like an array of colorful silks.
宾 (bīn) gives the sound — an exact match with 缤's reading.

example.hanzi: 公园里的花朵五彩缤纷。
example.pinyin: Gōngyuán lǐ de huāduǒ wǔcǎi-bīnfēn.
example.english: The flowers in the park are a riot of vivid colors.
example.fact: 缤纷 (bīnfēn), 'colorful, richly varied,' almost always pairs with 五彩 (wǔcǎi, 'five colors,' meaning a full spectrum) to form 五彩缤纷, one of the most common Chinese phrases for a scene bursting with color.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 嵋 names Mount Emei in Sichuan, written 峨嵋 or 峨眉.
眉 (méi) gives the sound — an exact match with 嵋's reading.

example.hanzi: 峨嵋山是中国四大佛教名山之一。
example.pinyin: Éméi Shān shì Zhōngguó sìdà Fójiào míngshān zhī yī.
example.english: Mount Emei is one of China's Four Great Buddhist Mountains.
example.fact: 嵋 exists almost solely to write the name of Mount Emei (峨嵋/峨眉), one of the Four Sacred Buddhist Mountains of China and a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its biodiversity and resident macaque monkeys.

components.note: 王 (a form of 玉, jade) — 珑 describes finely carved jade, especially pieces that produce a tinkling sound.
龙 (lóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 珑's reading.

example.hanzi: 这件玉雕玲珑精致。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yùdiāo línglóng jīngzhì.
example.english: This jade carving is exquisite and delicate.
example.fact: 玲珑 (línglóng), 'delicate, exquisite, finely wrought,' originally described the pleasant tinkling sound of jade ornaments knocking together, before broadening to describe delicate craftsmanship in general.

etymologyHint: A flower 艹 unfolding 包; 包 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 苞 names a plant's protective outer leaf, a bud calyx, or a firm rush-like plant.
包 (to wrap, to enclose) shares 苞's exact reading bāo, and its meaning of 'wrapping' reinforces the image of a bud enclosing a flower before it opens.

example.hanzi: 花苞还没有完全打开。
example.pinyin: Huābāo hái méiyǒu wánquán dǎkāi.
example.english: The flower bud hasn't fully opened yet.
example.fact: 花苞 (huābāo), 'flower bud,' names the protective covering of leaf-like tissue that wraps and protects a flower before it blooms.

components.note: 王 (a form of 玉, jade) — 瑾 describes fine, beautiful jade.
堇 (jǐn) gives the sound — an exact match with 瑾's reading.

example.hanzi: 瑾是一个常见于人名的字。
example.pinyin: Jǐn shì yí gè chángjiàn yú rénmíng de zì.
example.english: Jǐn is a character commonly seen in given names.
example.fact: 瑾 is often paired with 瑜 (yú, another 'fine jade' character) in Chinese given names — both simply mean 'beautiful jade,' reflecting an old habit of using precious stones as metaphors for admirable character in personal names.

etymologyHint: To pull water 水 out of stone 石

components.note: 泵 is a modern character, coined in the 20th century to write the loanword 'pump' — 石 (stone/rock) sits over 水 (water) in a purely invented combination, with a new reading, bèng, that doesn't derive from either part's traditional pronunciation.

example.hanzi: 这台泵用来把水抽到楼顶的水箱。
example.pinyin: Zhè tái bèng yòng lái bǎ shuǐ chōu dào lóudǐng de shuǐxiāng.
example.english: This pump is used to draw water up to the rooftop water tank.
example.fact: 泵 is one of a small set of Chinese characters invented in the 20th century purely to represent a loanword's sound and meaning — much like 甭 (béng, 'no need to'), tailored to modern needs rather than inherited from antiquity.
